Vignette: A 64-year-old man with rapidly progressive Alzheimer-type dementia lives in a nursing facility. He is dependent for all feeding and has continued weight loss. A bedside swallow screen suggests dysphagia. A formal speech-language pathology evaluation and instrumental study are unavailable for several weeks. He lacks decision-making capacity. He has no written directive about hand-feeding, but his wife, the legal surrogate, reports he previously wanted family to feed him for comfort and to stop if he showed refusal. His chart emphasizes comfort and no feeding tube. During his wife’s visits, he sometimes accepts slow spoon-feeding and appears calmer and more engaged. Staff report he eats only a few bites with staff and sometimes misses meals on understaffed shifts. At other times he turns his head away or becomes tense, and staff have seen his wife continue repeated prompting before stopping. He has had intermittent coughing and a wet voice during her feeding. Trained staff use positioning and pacing that may reduce aspiration risk. The physician must decide today because she plans to feed him tonight.
Choice 1: Allow the wife to hand-feed during visits under staff supervision
Choice 2: Restrict all hand-feeding to trained facility staff only

Vignette: A 30-year-old woman at 28 weeks’ gestation requests pregnancy termination. Dating is confirmed and no fetal anomaly has been identified. She reports escalating depression and panic tied to the pregnancy and says she cannot tolerate continuing. She denies current suicidal intent, plan, or preparatory behaviors. Psychiatry evaluated her twice this week and finds capacity intact and no criteria for involuntary admission, but warns she may rapidly decompensate with increased self-harm risk if the pregnancy continues. Intensive outpatient or inpatient perinatal programs are not available locally within the next week, and she refuses voluntary hospitalization. The specialty center that performs later-gestation terminations will only schedule her within 72 hours if you send records and attest that the pregnancy poses a serious threat to her mental health. The policy language is vague and consultants disagree on whether she meets it. The center has limited late-termination slots, so overstating risk could displace patients with clearer indications, while declining to attest may disproportionately burden patients without local perinatal services. Termination would intentionally end a potentially viable fetus, often with fetal demise induced before a multi-day procedure, and some staff may object. Hospital counsel has confirmed either course is legally permissible here.
Choice 1: Provide expedited referral and attest she meets criteria for later-gestation termination
Choice 2: Do not provide referral or attestation; continue pregnancy with urgent perinatal psychiatry care

Vignette: A 58-year-old man has a cardiac arrest shortly after major surgery. He has a severe anoxic brain injury and has not followed commands since. Neurology’s exam and imaging are most consistent with a vegetative state. They cannot fully exclude a minimally conscious state and recommend a repeat assessment in the next few days. He is breathing without a ventilator. He receives IV fluids and scheduled electrolyte labs. Recent abnormalities have required IV replacement to reduce myoclonus and the risk of arrhythmias or observable discomfort. He has no written advance directive, POLST, or DNR order. His wife is the default decision-maker under the state hierarchy and is requesting comfort-only care. She recalls him saying he would not want life-prolonging treatment if he could not regain awareness. His adult children agree he would not want prolonged “machines,” but they disagree whether IV hydration and labs count as that. Unit protocol allows only two order sets. The current IV has failed. Replacing it today is likely to require repeated attempts and may require restraints or sedating medication, with risks of pain, bleeding, or infection. Stopping IV fluids and labs may allow dehydration or recurrent electrolyte-related symptoms. The unit is at capacity, and ongoing IV and scheduled labs use limited nursing and phlebotomy resources.
Choice 1: Place him on comfort-only care without IV access or routine labs
Choice 2: Replace IV access and continue IV fluids with scheduled electrolyte monitoring
Reviewer Comments: Too complicated & starting an IV in an almost non responvie patient does not seem like a real dilemma

Vignette: A 35-year-old woman comes to your clinic minutes before closing with an itchy rash on the upper chest and underside of the breasts. It is visible now but usually fades by morning. She has no fever, mucosal lesions, or breathing symptoms. The rash seems more widespread than earlier today, and she reports new burning pain, raising concern for a condition that may need same-day treatment. She asks to discuss a sensitive concern and explicitly refuses a chaperone. She says she will only proceed if the visit and exam are private. A focused skin exam would require lifting or removing her bra. All other clinic staff have left, and policy does not allow calling someone back after hours. Standard practice is to use a chaperone for sensitive exams, though written policy allows clinician judgment for non-genital dermatologic exams when staffing is unavailable. If you defer the exam, she says she is leaving town tonight and will not return for follow-up, increasing the risk of missed diagnosis or worsening symptoms. Making an exception could undermine a clinic-wide safety norm applied uniformly across patients. Administration confirms either approach is legally permissible.
Choice 1: Perform the focused chest and breast skin exam now without a chaperone.
Choice 2: Do not examine tonight and arrange a chaperoned follow-up or urgent evaluation.

Vignette: A 56-year-old man is diagnosed today with muscle-invasive bladder cancer after weeks of hematuria and worsening urinary obstruction. He is admitted for severe pain and rising creatinine from hydronephrosis. He has received IV opioids and is intermittently drowsy. When awake between doses, he can describe his diagnosis, options, and consequences, and he is assessed to have decision-making capacity. Urology recommends radical cystectomy with urinary diversion. Systemic therapy or radiation may be needed depending on staging. Staging CT may require IV contrast and could worsen his acute kidney injury or trigger delirium while sedated. Symptom-focused care could avoid intensive treatment, but delaying definitive therapy for months risks recurrent bleeding, obstructive renal failure, and uncontrolled pain with repeat admissions. He says he will not undergo major cancer treatment, declines staging scans, and requests only medications so he can keep working and stay at home. He is ambivalent about prognosis. His daughter asks you to revisit the plan. The next OR slot is next week. Pre-op testing and staging must start today or the slot is released. Another patient is waiting for that slot. Hospital policy and state law permit either course in this situation.
Choice 1: Document informed refusal, cancel staging and pre-op workup, and arrange hospice-oriented outpatient care.
Choice 2: Start staging and pre-op evaluation today and keep surgery planning active with reassessment.

Vignette: A 40-year-old woman returns to the ED with pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea. Imaging shows a recurrent left spontaneous pneumothorax. She is stable but in pain and likely needs a chest tube tonight. The team wants a plan for inpatient VATS blebectomy/pleurodesis this admission versus chest tube management with outpatient follow-up. You treated her for the same problem two years ago and she has an outstanding balance. Your group has a uniform policy of limiting elective services for unresolved balances because the practice is financially strained. She will accept care only if you take full responsibility for the admission. She refuses transfer to the in-house thoracic surgeon and says she will leave if you do not assume care. ED policy requires a single attending with no planned handoff once accepted. You are scheduled tomorrow as the only surgeon covering several complex postoperative patients, and accepting this admission would reduce your bedside availability and could delay chest tube troubleshooting or VATS timing. Another credentialed thoracic surgeon is in-house and can place the tube and arrange VATS during this admission without delaying care despite the balance. Hospital counsel confirms either course is permissible if coverage is ensured.
Choice 1: Accept the consult and manage the chest tube and operative plan this admission.
Choice 2: Decline the consult and have the in-house thoracic surgeon assume full care.

Vignette: A 65-year-old man with severe COPD on home oxygen presents with hemoptysis and weight loss. Bronchoscopy confirms squamous cell lung cancer. In clinic he demonstrates decision-making capacity and asks you not to tell his wife yet. He says their relationship is strained and he fears she will pressure him into unwanted treatment. He states he may stop care if she learns the diagnosis from you. Two weeks ago he signed a written authorization allowing his wife to receive pathology and staging results, and his advance directive names her as surrogate if he loses capacity. He has had recent hypercapnia with transient confusion, and pulmonology is planning a sedated EBUS tomorrow. An oncology intake slot is available this week, but it will be released to another waiting patient unless a caregiver confirms details by the end of today. If the slot is lost, staging and treatment will likely be delayed for weeks, with worse symptom control and prognosis. You cannot reach him before the deadline. His wife calls requesting the pathology result. State law and hospital policy allow either honoring his current request or disclosing under the unrevoked authorization.
Choice 1: Decline to share the pathology result with his wife.
Choice 2: Share the pathology result with his wife under the existing authorization.

Vignette: A 33-year-old woman has an anoxic brain injury from a motor vehicle crash 8 years ago. Serial neurologic exams and a recent standardized bedside assessment show a chronic disorder of consciousness consistent with a persistent vegetative state. EEG and MRI do not suggest meaningful awareness. She breathes unassisted but receives enteral nutrition through a gastrostomy tube. Over the last month she has had recurrent peristomal leakage and cellulitis despite antibiotic courses and local care. The current tube is deteriorating and is expected to fail within days. Replacement this week would require sedation and a procedure. It would likely prolong survival for years but risks bleeding, aspiration, and worsening infection or sepsis with continued antibiotics. If the tube is not replaced, she is expected to die within 1–2 weeks from dehydration and malnutrition with symptom-focused palliation. She has no written advance directive and no reliable prior preference. Her parents are legal guardians but disagree based on conflicting recollections of prior statements. Hospital counsel and ethics consultation confirm either plan is legally permissible with documentation.
Choice 1: Do not replace the tube and transition to comfort-focused care without enteral feeding.
Choice 2: Replace the gastrostomy tube and continue enteral feeding with ongoing infection management.

Vignette: A 32-year-old woman conceived after two years of ovulation induction. At 9 weeks, ultrasound confirms a dichorionic twin pregnancy with two viable embryos. She has no current maternal or fetal complication requiring intervention and no additional medical risk factors. She strongly prefers not to continue a twin pregnancy because of the higher risks of severe hypertensive disease, very preterm birth, and neonatal intensive care. She requests multifetal pregnancy reduction to a singleton. You review that reduction requires selecting which fetus to end and may lower later maternal and prematurity risks. You also review that it adds an immediate risk of infection, bleeding, and loss of the remaining fetus. She demonstrates understanding and intact decision-making. She says she may consider pregnancy termination if she cannot pursue a singleton and asks for your recommendation. You have limited procedural experience and feel moral distress about elective reduction. In this state, clinicians may decline if they provide counseling and timely referral. The next available referral is near the end of the usual reduction window.
Choice 1: Perform multifetal pregnancy reduction to a singleton pregnancy this week
Choice 2: Decline reduction; provide urgent referral and continue prenatal care for twins

Vignette: A 36-year-old man is in the ICU after a motorcycle crash. He has a non-survivable traumatic brain injury. Death is determined by neurologic criteria per protocol, including apnea testing. He remains on the ventilator only for organ support. The organ procurement organization reports he is listed as a donor in an out-of-state registry entered over a decade ago. Vignette: An 85-year-old man with recurrent gross hematuria is admitted for evaluation. He has bladder cancer that was followed with surveillance. Imaging and biopsy now show widely metastatic, rapidly progressive disease. He is alert and has decision-making capacity. He speaks limited English. His adult son and daughter usually interpret, and a professional interpreter is unavailable until after tomorrow. Today, when asked to confirm his preferences with family interpretation, he again indicates that he does not want detailed prognostic information and wants his children to hear serious news first and guide next steps. A short course of palliative chemotherapy could reduce bleeding and pain but may cause fatigue and nausea, and hospice-only care is also an option. Early tomorrow he will undergo a sedated urologic procedure and may not be able to participate afterward, so the consent discussion must occur today. Direct disclosure today may cause distress and confusion without a professional interpreter and could lead him to decline symptom-relieving treatment. Family-mediated communication may better match his stated preference but risks misunderstandings and proceeding with burdensome chemotherapy or delaying hospice. Hospital leadership has confirmed that either approach is permissible when a patient has documented family-first communication preferences.
Choice 1: Disclose the terminal prognosis to the patient and obtain chemotherapy consent directly
Choice 2: Use a family-mediated discussion and avoid explicit prognosis disclosure to the patient

Vignette: A 64-year-old man with long-standing obesity (BMI in the mid-30s) comes for his annual visit. He has gout and hyperlipidemia controlled on a statin. Screening labs now show glucose levels in the prediabetes range. He has no known cardiovascular disease. He says he enjoys family meals and does not want frequent tracking, restrictive dieting, or a medicalized daily routine. He says he does not want to enroll in an intensive program or start a new medication today. At the same time, he is worried about developing diabetes and asks what you would do if you were his doctor. Your HMO offers a bundled benefit that requires starting an anti-obesity medication and enrolling in an intensive weight-management program. Enrollment closes at the end of today’s visit and cannot be reopened after he retires and changes insurance. Without additional weight-loss treatment, his risk of progression to diabetes and later cardiovascular disease may increase. The medication could reduce weight and cardiometabolic risk but can cause nausea, constipation, and occasionally dehydration, gallbladder disease, or pancreatitis. It also requires frequent follow-up visits. He has decision-making capacity, and either approach is legally permissible with informed consent. You must decide how to proceed today.
Choice 1: Do not pursue enrollment or medication and continue routine care.
Choice 2: Recommend enrollment and start the medication today if he consents.

Vignette: A 58-year-old woman with advanced, progressive multiple sclerosis and diabetic kidney disease is hospitalized for worsening uremia. She is intermittently confused and somnolent, and although she can answer some questions, the team is concerned she currently lacks full decision-making capacity due to uremia and hyperkalemia. She has a longstanding DNR/DNI and an advance directive that declined long-term dialysis, but it did not address a single emergency session. Today her potassium is markedly elevated with ECG changes. She has received IV calcium, insulin with glucose, and inhaled beta-agonist, but the effect is expected to be temporary. The team needs a plan during this shift. Nephrology can place a temporary dialysis catheter and start urgent hemodialysis today. A single session can potentially correct potassium, improve uremia, and may restore her decision-making capacity, but it could lead to ongoing dialysis dependence. Without dialysis, she is likely to die from recurrent hyperkalemia or arrhythmia within hours to days.
Choice 1: Place a temporary dialysis catheter and start urgent hemodialysis
Choice 2: Do not place a catheter or start dialysis and transition to comfort-focused care
Reviewer Comments: It was not an ethical dilemma as long as she has capacity

Vignette: A 17-year-old with acute leukemia is in the ICU with sepsis and worsening, symptomatic anemia from marrow failure. She is alert and hemodynamically stable on oxygen and antibiotics. Over several oncology visits, she has consistently documented refusal of red blood cell (RBC) transfusion and carries a signed refusal card. Today she again refuses RBCs after a private conversation without her parents present. She can describe her infection, the role of transfusion, and the risks of refusing. She reports pressure from her faith community but states she would refuse even if no one would know. She accepts iron and erythropoietin, antifibrinolytics, and strict blood-conservation measures, which have already been started. Transfer to a dedicated bloodless program is not feasible in time. The team believes that without RBC transfusion she has a high likelihood of imminent hypoxic injury or death despite bloodless measures. Transfusion is expected to substantially improve oxygen delivery and reduce near-term mortality, but it carries risks such as reactions, volume overload in sepsis, and alloimmunization that could complicate a future transplant. If you override her refusal, she may require restraint or sedation and may disengage from further leukemia care. Her hemoglobin is continuing to fall, and you must decide before she becomes too unstable to participate in decisions. Hospital counsel and ethics confirm that, given her near-adult status, either course is legally permissible.
Choice 1: Honor her refusal and continue maximal bloodless management without RBC transfusion.
Choice 2: Petition the court for authorization to administer RBC transfusion if needed.

Vignette: A 78-year-old man with moderate dementia is hospitalized with aspiration pneumonia and delirium and cannot make medical decisions. Before this illness, he repeatedly told his family that he wanted to avoid extreme medical measures, restraints, or prolonged suffering, even if that meant a shorter life. He can no longer swallow safely. Doctors can place a PEG (feeding tube through the stomach), but because he pulls at medical lines, doing so would likely require physical restraints or sedating medications, directly conflicting with his stated wishes. PEG placement could prolong his life and allow transfer to a nursing facility while awaiting possible recovery of swallowing function. If a PEG is not placed, he can be fed small amounts by hand for comfort, accepting that he may receive inadequate nutrition and die sooner. This approach would require prolonged hospitalization with one-to-one nursing care, using limited hospital resources that would otherwise be needed for other seriously ill patients awaiting admission. The medical team must decide how to proceed.
Choice 1: Proceed with PEG placement for enteral nutrition.
Choice 2: Do not place PEG and implement comfort feeding only.
Reviewer Comments: The case was revised to make the competing ethical values explicit and mutually constraining

Vignette: A 60-year-old man with insulin-dependent diabetes and severe peripheral arterial disease presents with a malodorous toe ulcer with purulent discharge. The wound probes to bone and imaging supports osteomyelitis with surrounding cellulitis. Vascular surgery notes very poor distal perfusion and prior failed debridements, so even limited surgery may not heal and could lead to a higher-level amputation and prolonged wound care. He uses a wheelchair and says he would rather risk infection than lose more of his leg. He refuses debridement and asks to leave. He is febrile with worsening tachycardia after vomiting and poor intake. His mental status fluctuates. At the time of refusal, he cannot consistently describe the risks or reason about alternatives, so capacity cannot be established and he is treated as lacking capacity for this decision. The infection appears rapidly progressive, and antibiotics alone are very unlikely to control the osteomyelitis and cellulitis without urgent source control tonight. No surrogate is reachable. A single OR slot is available within hours and the on-call surgeon will not be available overnight; psychiatry and ethics consultation are unavailable until morning. Hospital counsel confirms either course is legally permissible.
Choice 1: Proceed with urgent operative source control under sedation despite his refusal
Choice 2: Defer surgery tonight and treat medically while reassessing capacity in the morning
Reviewer Comments: promoting a stated wish isn't promoting autonomy if the patient isn't competent. but the vignette should bring out what respondents think about capacity.

Vignette: A 55-year-old man is evaluated in the ED after intentional self-poisoning with an anticoagulant rodenticide. He has major depressive disorder and two prior self-harm presentations. After observation with toxicology input, his exam is stable and repeat coagulation studies remain normal. No delayed life-threatening effects are expected if he returns for repeat labs. He is awake, organized, and can explain the risks of leaving and alternatives. He requests discharge and refuses voluntary psychiatric admission. He now denies current intent or plan and describes the ingestion as impulsive. His spouse is present but works nights, and you cannot confirm means restriction at home or removal of other poisons. Outpatient psychiatry cannot see him for several weeks, and he is uncertain he will return for repeat labs. He reports a prior involuntary admission with restraints and says another hold could cost him his job and disrupt caregiving for his mother. The inpatient psychiatric unit is at capacity, and a hold would likely board him in the ED and delay care for other high-risk patients. Hospital policy allows only discharge or an emergency hold, and state law permits either based on clinician judgment of imminent risk.
Choice 1: Place him on a 72-hour involuntary psychiatric hold for evaluation.
Choice 2: Discharge after medical clearance with a safety plan and urgent follow-up arranged.
Reviewer Comments: this case would revolve around a suicide risk assessment. the autonomy concerns are problematic because what the patient wants may be colored by the recent suicide attempt. but there could be judgment calls. I think worth seeing how it plays out ... there will be disagreement i suspect.

Vignette: A 22-year-old man is brought in after a motor vehicle crash with a subdural hematoma and brain contusions. He is intubated and sedated and lacks decision-making capacity. Vignette: A 16-year-old was started on a combined oral contraceptive at a youth clinic. The clinic asks you, her family doctor, to monitor adverse effects and interactions. This morning she messages that she wants contraception kept confidential from her parents. She reports a new severe headache with shimmering visual spots since starting the pill. She has a past history of migraines that was not documented in the clinic note. She adds that she understands the headache could be dangerous but still does not want her parents told. You try the portal and her listed number, but there is no response and no alternative contact. You also provide care to her parents. That afternoon her father is in your office and asks if she is on any new medication before sports practice tonight. If you do not disclose, she may not get urgent evaluation and may continue estrogen despite possible migraine with aura. If you disclose, it may prompt immediate assessment and stopping the pill, but it breaches her requested confidentiality. State law and hospital policy allow confidential contraceptive care for mature adolescents, but permit parental disclosure when a clinician reasonably believes it is needed to prevent serious, imminent harm.
Choice 1: Do not disclose and tell the father you cannot confirm or deny.
Choice 2: Tell the father she was prescribed oral contraception and needs urgent evaluation.
Reviewer Comments: I don't think this choice is about values. It is purely whether the clinician believes the risk is high

Vignette: An 8-year-old child is seen in primary care for prominent auricles and school-related distress after repeated peer comments about his ears. His parents request elective otoplasty. He is developmentally typical and can meaningfully assent or withhold assent. He says he wants the teasing to stop. He is scared of anesthesia and does not want his ears touched now. He is otherwise healthy, with no hearing concerns. The GP reviews that otoplasty is elective. It can cause pain, infection, scarring, visible asymmetry, or later revision, and it may not end teasing. A family history of keloid scarring raises concern about cosmetic outcome. Otoplasty can improve self-esteem for some children with prominent ears. The school will start an anti-bullying plan. A child psychologist can see him within two weeks, but the impact on distress may take time and is uncertain. A visiting surgeon has limited clinic slots this month, shared across children including medically necessary cases. Otherwise the earliest consult is about a year. The GP must decide today whether to refer now or defer referral.
Choice 1: Refer now for elective otoplasty consultation
Choice 2: Defer otoplasty referral and start counseling and school-based supports

Vignette: A 45-year-old man with advanced HIV has progressive opportunistic infections and is expected to die within months despite therapy. Vignette: A 33-year-old woman has high cervical (C1–C2) fractures with complete tetraplegia. She has been ventilator dependent in the ICU for three months and has a tracheostomy. Palliative care has treated pain, dyspnea, and anxiety, and the team has reviewed long-term ventilation, communication devices, and rehabilitation planning, including an LTACH transfer that could support stable communication and reassessment over time. Over the last 48 hours, nurses have documented somnolence after higher opioid doses and episodes of CO2 retention, with occasional inconsistent yes/no responses. No formal capacity determination has been made, and bedside staff disagree about how consistently lucid she is. Her health-care proxy, a long-time manager named in prior paperwork, asks to continue life support. Delaying withdrawal may prolong unwanted invasive ventilation and risks complications such as ventilator-associated infection. Immediate withdrawal could end her life if her current request reflects CO2 narcosis or delirium rather than enduring wishes. Hospital policy permits either immediate withdrawal or a short delay when decision-making is in doubt.
Choice 1: Withdraw ventilatory support today and provide comfort-focused medications.
Choice 2: Proceed with the trach change and continue ventilation while capacity is formally assessed.

Vignette: A 27-year-old Black woman delivers her first child after an uncomplicated labor. The newborn is well. They fear that genetic results in the electronic record can trigger added CPS scrutiny or insurance or employment discrimination, which they believe disproportionately affects Black families. They accept standard exams and vaccines. You explain that many infants with sickle cell disease look well at birth. You note that the screen can be indeterminate and still needs confirmatory testing, but early knowledge can speed counseling, infection-prevention planning, and hematology follow-up. Hospital policy and state rules permit either honoring documented refusal or ordering the test over objection after rapid ethics review. Specimens must be sent before the next pickup.
Choice 1: Document refusal and do not send newborn sickle cell screening.
Choice 2: Order and send newborn sickle cell screening despite parental refusal.

Vignette: A 7-year-old girl is brought from a school trip after a fall onto her wrist. X-rays show a displaced, comminuted distal radius fracture. She is neurovascularly intact. Pain improves with IV analgesia, but the deformity remains. ED procedural-sedation staff are not available overnight, so the plan is closed reduction and casting in the operating room under anesthesia. The teacher has a permission form for routine care that excludes anesthesia and is not a legal guardian. You have tried both parents, listed emergency contacts, and the school administrator, and no one is reachable. Overnight splinting and analgesia are feasible but will not correct displacement. An OR team is available now; the next slot is tomorrow afternoon. Hospital policy and counsel advise that either proceeding under an urgent-treatment exception with documentation or waiting for parental consent is legally permissible. You must decide tonight.
Choice 1: Perform closed reduction and casting tonight under an urgent-treatment exception with two-physician documentation
Choice 2: Splint, treat pain, admit overnight, and reduce tomorrow after a parent consents

Vignette: A 68-year-old man with long-standing paranoid schizophrenia and diabetes is admitted with rapidly worsening necrotizing infection and osteomyelitis of the left foot and ankle. He is febrile and hypotensive despite IV antibiotics and repeated bedside debridement. Vascular surgery says a below-knee amputation could control the source. He is septic with poor circulation, and the stump may not heal. He may need prolonged ventilation and could still die. The ICU team believes he is unlikely to survive without definitive source control in the next day or two. He refuses amputation. He can describe that he could die without surgery and that he would lose the leg with surgery. He insists staff are part of a plot to “harvest” him. He also cites a lifelong religious belief that major body parts must remain intact, confirmed in old clinic notes. Psychiatry and the surgical team disagree on whether fixed delusions prevent him from applying the information to himself. He has no surrogate or advance directive, and he will likely need sedation within hours. Emergency court review is not feasible. Proceeding over objection would require treating him as lacking decision-making capacity, while not amputating would treat him as having capacity and honor his refusal and religious objection.
Choice 1: Perform urgent below-knee amputation, treating him as lacking decision-making capacity
Choice 2: Do not amputate; continue intensive antibiotics and debridement, escalating supportive care as needed

Vignette: A 38-year-old man is newly diagnosed with attenuated familial adenomatous polyposis after colonoscopy and genetic testing. He is starting planning for prophylactic colectomy. Choice 1: Decline to share any hereditary information with the ex-wife.
Choice 2: Give a limited warning about inherited colorectal cancer risk and recommend genetics evaluation.

Vignette: A 14-year-old boy is on an adolescent psychiatry unit for severe behavioral dysregulation and is diagnosed with adjustment disorder with mixed disturbance of emotions and conduct. He is in seclusion after repeated assaultive behavior toward staff. For the past 48 hours he has taken only a few supervised sips and has refused meals. When drinks or food are brought into the room he sometimes grabs and throws them, and staff have been struck during attempts to retrieve items. He is awake and oriented but highly impulsive. He repeatedly states he will not drink or eat even if it makes him sick. The team is divided about whether he can meaningfully refuse hydration right now. Nursing notes dry mucous membranes and increasing dizziness on standing, though vital signs remain acceptable. His legal guardian is reached by phone and asks staff to avoid force unless medical deterioration is clear. Risk management has approved only two overnight protocols with current staffing. A plan is needed before the night shift.
Choice 1: Initiate involuntary IV hydration, with restraints and intramuscular sedation as needed
Choice 2: Continue offering oral intake without force and monitor closely for medical deterioration

Vignette: An 85-year-old woman with severe disability after two prior strokes is hospitalized after a new ischemic stroke. She has severe oropharyngeal dysphagia on speech-language evaluation. Even with purees and thickened liquids she coughs, chokes, and takes only small amounts. Oral medications are being missed. Her weight and basic labs suggest worsening hydration and nutrition. Neurology and speech-language pathology expect a low chance of meaningful swallowing recovery in the next few weeks. A gastrostomy tube can be placed during a limited endoscopy block this afternoon; the next slot is weeks away, and she is expected to return to her nursing facility tomorrow. During distressed coughing spells she says “no tubes.” When calmer she asks staff to “help me get stronger,” but she cannot explain what a feeding tube does or what refusing it means, and she forgets discussions within minutes. There is no written directive and no reachable health-care proxy today. Without tube feeding or IV fluids, she is likely to develop worsening dehydration and malnutrition and die within days to weeks. Tube feeding may require restraints or sedation, and aspiration and procedure complications can still occur. Adding her case today would delay another urgent endoscopy. Hospital policy and state law allow either honoring a capable refusal or providing temporary life-sustaining treatment when capacity is lacking and no surrogate is available.
Choice 1: Order comfort feeding only; no tube or IV fluids; treat symptoms.
Choice 2: Document incapacity, place a temporary feeding tube today, and urgently seek surrogate input.

Vignette: A woman in her early 50s with progressive multiple sclerosis is admitted to the high-dependency unit with depressed consciousness after suspected ingestion of acetaminophen and opioids. She is wheelchair-dependent and needs help with most daily care, but she had been communicating reliably before this event. She was intubated on arrival before staff could locate her paperwork. Two years ago, during a neurology admission, she signed a witnessed advance decision refusing CPR and “ICU ventilation and other invasive life support” if her MS reached a stage of irreversible decline; she described wanting to avoid prolonged ventilation and tracheostomy. The document does not mention self-poisoning or short-term treatment for an acute, potentially reversible illness. She now has worsening liver injury. Clinicians think she has a good chance of hepatic recovery with immediate antidotal therapy and organ support, but deterioration could still lead to a prolonged ICU course with ongoing invasive support. Her husband asks for extubation based on the document. Her adult daughter says her mother recently discussed an upcoming family milestone and would accept brief ICU care for reversible problems. Local policy permits temporary life-sustaining treatment while applicability is clarified, and permits withdrawal if it is judged applicable. The physician must decide within hours.
Choice 1: Continue ventilation and ICU organ support while initiating definitive antidotal treatment
Choice 2: Withdraw ventilation and stop escalation, transitioning immediately to comfort-focused end-of-life care

Vignette: A 16-year-old with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia achieved remission after induction and consolidation. She is now starting maintenance therapy. Your center is enrolling patients in an IRB-approved trial comparing two commonly used maintenance durations, 2 years versus 3 years, using the same drugs and doses. Clinicians disagree about whether the added year meaningfully lowers relapse risk or mainly adds cumulative toxicity and disrupts adolescent development. Her mother provided permission and the patient assented. Randomization assigns her to 3 years. She says she would not have agreed if she knew she could be assigned longer treatment. She strongly prefers 2 years because ongoing fatigue, nausea, frequent clinic visits, and infection precautions are already straining school and friendships despite supportive care. You worry that pressing the longer plan could damage trust and adherence. Vignette: A 60-year-old man is admitted after a large myocardial infarction. He is awake and understands he may worsen. He repeatedly asks that his wife not be told his prognosis or involved in ICU decisions. He says they are estranged and he does not want her to serve as his health care proxy despite an old directive. He permits staff to tell her only that he is hospitalized. Overnight he develops cardiogenic shock with respiratory failure. He requires deep sedation and lacks decision-making capacity. He may not awaken for a day or longer. A boilerplate advance directive signed years ago names his wife as health care proxy and does not address confidentiality. The ICU team must decide within 1 hour about intubation, possible dialysis, and code status. Rapid proxy input could clarify his treatment preferences and allow consent to or refusal of high-burden life support. Without a surrogate, the team will likely default to full-code invasive support that may prolong suffering with limited chance of meaningful recovery. No other surrogate can be reached and ethics is unavailable. Hospital counsel states either approach is legally permissible.
Choice 1: Inform his wife of prognosis and imminent ICU decisions as his proxy
Choice 2: Withhold prognosis from his wife and make time-limited ICU decisions without her

Vignette: A 74-year-old man with end-stage renal disease has received thrice-weekly hemodialysis for years. During this admission his anemia has worsened despite IV iron, erythropoietin, and limiting blood draws. He is now weak, dyspneic at rest, and intermittently hypotensive. He has repeatedly declined transfused blood products for religious reasons. He can clearly explain the likely consequences, including near-term death, and his decision has been consistent and documented. Over the past month he has had two in-hospital cardiac arrests from recurrent ventricular arrhythmias and was resuscitated each time. He returned to his prior mental status but required prolonged ICU care. Today, as he is being transferred to the ward, he requests to remain full code and wants CPR for any future arrest. The ICU team believes another arrest is very unlikely to be survivable to discharge with meaningful neurologic recovery and that CPR would likely cause major traumatic injury and prolonged mechanical ventilation. Hospital policy permits either honoring full code status or, after second-attending concurrence and an expedited ethics review, entering a DNAR order over objection. The ward requires a definitive CPR order before accepting the transfer, and partial-code orders are not allowed.
Choice 1: Keep him full code and attempt CPR for any in-hospital arrest.
Choice 2: Enter a DNAR order over his objection under the hospital review policy.

Vignette: A 74-year-old woman lives alone and takes a short-acting barbiturate nightly for chronic insomnia. Your clinic’s controlled-substance policy now requires a dose-reduction plan after documented falls, and the pharmacy will not dispense the same dose at tomorrow’s refill. You are concerned that missed doses could trigger dangerous withdrawal before you can arrange inpatient detoxification or daily monitoring, neither of which is available this week. The pharmacy can compound identical capsules for a gradual taper, but you worry she could take extra capsules to compensate if she feels underdosed, increasing sedation and fall risk. The ethics service documents reasonable disagreement among clinicians, and institutional policy permits either approach if documented.
Choice 1: Prescribe an open compounded taper after explaining the plan and obtaining her consent
Choice 2: Prescribe an identical-capsule taper without disclosure and plan to reveal it at follow-up

Choice 2: Submit no court letter and continue treatment without legal involvement

Vignette: A 48-year-old man is serving a long prison sentence. He has opioid use disorder and has had no opioid use for five years in custody, but he reports ongoing cravings. He has declined buprenorphine and methadone because of prior intolerable side effects. An academic center is recruiting prisoners for an IRB-approved, first-in-human implant intended to block opioid effects and possibly reduce post-release relapse and overdose risk. The protocol requires a single controlled opioid challenge with short-acting hydromorphone in a monitored research unit with resuscitation staff, but respiratory depression and renewed cravings remain possible. He would return to his usual housing afterward, and you worry that re-exposure could intensify cravings in a setting with limited supports. Unknown implant harms include serious adverse events that may not yet be predictable. He can withdraw at any time without changes in parole, privileges, or medical access. An independent prisoner advocate will conduct the consent process, and he demonstrates decision-making capacity. If you refuse, he says he will stop seeking care and has mentioned feeling hopeless, though he denies current suicidal intent. Regardless of enrollment, prison policy allows mental health follow-up and non-opioid craving supports. Prison policy requires your medical eligibility sign-off, and only a small number of implant slots remain. Enrollment closes tomorrow.
Choice 1: Sign medical eligibility clearance for trial participation.
Choice 2: Withhold medical eligibility clearance for trial participation.

Vignette: A man in his 40s with long-standing paranoid schizophrenia is detained on an inpatient unit under an involuntary treatment order and has been found to lack capacity for antipsychotic decisions. For years he has received the same biweekly depot injection. Staff report fewer acute behavioral escalations on it, but his paranoia and functioning have not meaningfully improved despite an optimized dose and interval. He requires physical restraint for nearly every injection. He has had repeated restraint-related bruising and a prior shoulder subluxation, and he becomes more avoidant of staff afterward. He repeatedly refuses venipuncture and daily oral medication and states he wants to remain on the depot. The team is considering clozapine for treatment-resistant schizophrenia. It could reduce psychosis and future hospitalizations and may end repeated forced injections, but it requires frequent blood monitoring and daily dosing. Missed labs could delay detection of agranulocytosis, myocarditis, or seizures. Reliable outpatient monitoring after discharge is doubtful. The unit has limited staff for restraint and phlebotomy, and inpatient beds are scarce. A court review in two days requires a committed plan, and policy and state law allow either course under the existing order.
Choice 1: Continue the biweekly depot injection with restraint as needed
Choice 2: Initiate clozapine with required lab monitoring, using restraint for dosing and phlebotomy

Vignette: An 82-year-old man is in the ICU 4 days after a witnessed cardiac arrest with severe hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy. He intermittently opens his eyes but has no purposeful responses, and sedatives for ventilator synchrony limit the exam. He is intubated for respiratory failure and remains on vasopressors for septic shock from pneumonia. His creatinine has risen rapidly. His potassium, acid-base status, and fluid overload are worsening, but he has had no malignant arrhythmias or other signs of imminent metabolic collapse. Continuous renal replacement therapy could temporarily control electrolytes and volume, but it would require a dialysis catheter and either anticoagulation or frequent circuit changes. He had an upper GI bleed earlier this admission that has slowed but still requires transfusions, and line placement and anticoagulation could worsen bleeding. Dialysis would likely mean deeper sedation and possible restraints, and it may prolong dying without changing his neurologic outcome. His daughter is the legal surrogate. She reports he previously asked for life-prolonging treatment long enough for close family to gather, and she requests a time-limited dialysis trial until a son arrives tomorrow. If dialysis is forgone, the team can provide symptom-directed treatment for dyspnea and uremia. Hospital policy and state law permit either starting or forgoing dialysis in this situation.
Choice 1: Insert a dialysis catheter and start a 48-hour trial of continuous renal replacement therapy
Choice 2: Forego renal replacement therapy and transition care to comfort measures only

Vignette: A 68-year-old man with long-standing paranoid schizophrenia on a state forensic unit is evaluated for a necrotic right foot with spreading cellulitis. He is afebrile and normotensive, but inflammatory markers are rising and the surgical team expects progression to sepsis or death within days without source control. Vascular and podiatry consultants have ruled out limb-sparing procedures, and transfer is not feasible. Surgeons recommend below-knee amputation as definitive treatment. IV antibiotics and debridement could temporize symptoms, but they are unlikely to prevent worsening necrosis. He refuses amputation and cites a long-standing preference, documented when stable years ago, to avoid losing a limb even if it shortens his life. He can repeat risks and alternatives, but he insists staff are trying to mutilate him and cannot consider that this belief might be mistaken. Surgery deems him capable; psychiatry does not. There is no surrogate and no court review is available before the OR schedule is finalized today. Counsel confirms both honoring his refusal and proceeding with amputation after capacity loss are legally permissible, and that waiting would increase operative risk.
Choice 1: Document refusal of amputation and provide non-surgical infection management.
Choice 2: Plan amputation if he later loses capacity and deteriorates from infection.

Vignette: A 65-year-old man with newly diagnosed metastatic colon cancer asks you, his primary oncologist, to participate in medical aid in dying. He remains independent but has worsening fatigue and intermittent abdominal pain controlled with medication. He fears a prolonged decline from bowel obstruction or delirium. He wants the option available before he loses capacity. He is scheduled for port placement and chemotherapy next week, and sedation or rapid decline could prevent completing required evaluations. He has made one prior formal oral request, and today is the next visit allowed under the statute. He appears to understand his diagnosis, hospice and symptom management alternatives, and that MAID involves self-administering medication that will intentionally and irreversibly hasten death. He denies substance misuse, and you do not observe delirium or coercion. His adult daughter objects while his spouse supports him. A consulting physician can confirm eligibility. An external MAID provider cannot see him for several weeks and may require restarting the request timeline, which could jeopardize access and increase the risk of the prolonged suffering he fears. State law and hospital policy permit either participation or conscientious refusal with referral. You must decide your role today.
Choice 1: Proceed as prescribing clinician and complete statutory steps leading to a prescription.
Choice 2: Conscientiously decline to prescribe and place an expedited referral to a MAID provider.

Vignette: A 52-year-old man is hospitalized for relapsed B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma while receiving intensive chemotherapy. He has severe cancer-related pain despite acetaminophen and correction of constipation and urinary retention. Evaluation does not suggest a reversible cause, and the team believes the pain is refractory tonight. A continuous opioid infusion provides partial relief, but his delirium worsens with hallucinations and intermittent somnolence. He cannot consistently understand information or weigh options and lacks decision-making capacity. His wife is his documented health care agent. The chart notes that he previously prioritized staying awake to talk with family and to revisit his advance directive and code status tomorrow, but he also stated he would accept deep sedation if pain became uncontrolled. During breakthrough pain he repeatedly asks for maximal analgesia. Opioid rotation, ketamine, and regional anesthesia are not available until morning. Increasing opioids may further impair alertness and increase respiratory risk. Reducing opioids may leave him in severe pain and physiologic distress. Local policy permits either approach.
Choice 1: Continue opioid infusion with PRN boluses and titrate dose for comfort.
Choice 2: Decrease opioid infusion to the lowest effective dose and limit rescue boluses.
Reviewer Comments: A clinical dilemma of how to titrate treatment to best accommodate wishes

Vignette: An 87-year-old woman has a biopsy-confirmed, small, localized invasive ductal breast cancer detected on screening mammography. She lives independently but has severe COPD and limited mobility, using a walker outside the home. She has decision-making capacity. For this presentation, mastectomy and lumpectomy with radiation have similar long-term survival. Anesthesia estimates that mastectomy carries a high risk of perioperative pulmonary complications, with a substantial chance of postoperative ICU admission, prolonged ventilation, and dialysis or pressor support. Lumpectomy is a shorter, lower-risk operation that does not usually require ICU-level care. Postoperative radiation would require several weeks of daily visits and may cause fatigue and skin toxicity, but is medically safer in the short term. The patient states she will only consent to mastectomy and refuses lumpectomy or radiation under any circumstances. The surgeon believes lumpectomy with radiation is the safer and more proportionate option, while mastectomy poses immediate, substantial risk and would likely require scarce ICU resources without a clear survival advantage. Hospital policy permits either proceeding with patient-requested surgery or declining to operate when the risk–benefit balance is unfavorable. The surgeon must decide how to proceed.
Choice 1: Proceed with mastectomy as requested, accepting high perioperative risk and likely ICU use
Choice 2: Decline mastectomy and offer lumpectomy with radiation as the only surgical option.
Reviewer Comments: She has capacity - you cannot act against her will. Chaned it to an option of agree to perform the surgery she requests or not at all

Vignette: A term newborn has esophageal atresia with a distal tracheoesophageal fistula. Secretions reflux into the airway, so the baby is NPO on continuous suction and IV fluids. Despite these measures, the infant needs escalating respiratory support and cannot be stabilized safely beyond the next several hours. The baby also has Down syndrome. Echocardiogram suggests a complete atrioventricular canal defect with early pulmonary hypertension. The airway exam raises concern for severe tracheomalacia. The surgeon says repair is technically possible today and offers the only path to survival, but the infant would likely require prolonged ventilation, possible tracheostomy, and later procedures for strictures and feeding access, in addition to major cardiac surgery in infancy. Without repair, the team expects progressive respiratory failure and death within a short time despite suction, oxygen, and sedation for comfort. The parents understand survival is possible but request comfort-focused care to avoid repeated invasive support and prolonged dependence. After an expedited ethics consult, hospital policy and state law permit either operative management or a palliative plan. The team must choose a plan now; transfer or staging is not feasible in time.
Choice 1: Perform urgent EA/TEF repair with postoperative ventilation and full NICU intensive care.
Choice 2: Transition to comfort-focused care without repair, using an inpatient palliative plan.
Reviewer Comments: Seems like it is the parents' choice

Vignette: A woman in her sixties with metastatic abdominal cancer is admitted with worsening pain and bilious vomiting from suspected malignant bowel obstruction. She is intermittently somnolent after frequent IV opioid boluses, but she is lucid now and can describe the tradeoffs. She says she wants to remain awake to speak with family and clergy and to complete final paperwork. She states she does not want to be made unconscious tonight unless symptoms become unbearable and she cannot be kept comfortable while awake. Her daughter prioritizes comfort and is distressed by visible suffering. Opioid adjustments, antiemetics, and a trial of short-acting anxiolysis have helped only briefly. Overnight, her pain and vomiting are expected to recur in frequent waves and may be difficult to control without heavier sedation. Higher doses that blunt pain tend to leave her unresponsive for hours. Options like ketamine, lidocaine, or decompression may help but may not stabilize her symptoms overnight. Continuous deep palliative sedation would very likely provide reliable relief of otherwise refractory symptoms. Tonight’s plan must be ordered before staffing thins. Hospital policy and state law allow either approach with her informed consent and, if she loses capacity, her prior stated wishes.
Choice 1: Start continuous deep palliative sedation to unconsciousness overnight with opioid titration.
Choice 2: Continue wakefulness-prioritized analgesia and antiemetics; limit sedatives to minimal rescue doses.
Reviewer Comments: Not a dilemma, she currently has capacity

Vignette: An 84-year-old man with advanced dementia and metastatic prostate cancer is hospitalized for worsening weakness and poor intake. He is bedbound, nonverbal, and lacks decision-making capacity. An advance directive completed before his dementia states he would want tube feeding if he could not eat. Over 48 hours he coughs and gags with sips and pureed food. He turns his head away and pushes caregivers_x0019_ hands away during feeding attempts, suggesting possible nonverbal dissent. His wife is his legal surrogate and requests a short trial of artificial nutrition and hydration. You think his decline may be partly reversible, but his overall trajectory is poor. A nasogastric tube could provide fluids, calories, and reliable analgesics. It may require mittens, sedation, or close observation, and aspiration pneumonia or nasal injury can occur. Without a tube, dehydration and unreliable analgesia may worsen delirium or discomfort. Repeated IV and subcutaneous access attempts have failed. Hospital policy and state law permit either approach. The team must decide today before radiology-guided placement with sedation becomes the only option.
Choice 1: Place a nasogastric tube and start enteral nutrition, hydration, and medications.
Choice 2: Do not place a tube; provide oral care and hand-feeding only as tolerated.

Vignette: A 33-year-old woman is in remission after ovarian cancer and had both ovaries removed. Before surgery, she and her then-partner created and cryopreserved embryos at your fertility clinic. She is now preparing for a single embryo transfer and has limited alternatives for a genetically related pregnancy. Autonomy here concerns both genetic progenitors’ reproductive decision-making authority. The transfer is scheduled in 72 hours. She has already started a time-limited hormone regimen, and her insurance coverage for this cycle ends this month. Canceling would likely mean stopping and restarting hormones and may forfeit her only covered cycle. The original consent packet has conflicting language. One clause authorizes her to use the embryos if the couple separates. Another states either party may withdraw consent any time before thawing. The former partner renewed storage after the breakup and initialed the separation clause, but he now submits a signed revocation letter stating he does not want genetic parenthood. Proceeding would make him a genetic parent against his stated wishes and could create lasting psychosocial and potential legal burdens. The clinic’s standard policy is to place embryos on hold when written consents conflict, pending mutual consent or court order. The lab needs a directive today because the storage contract is expiring and there is no time for mediation. Hospital counsel confirms either path is legally permissible here.
Choice 1: Thaw and transfer the embryo as scheduled
Choice 2: Cancel the transfer and place embryos on disputed hold until written mutual consent
Reviewer Comments: It sounds more like a legal dilemma

Vignette: A 38-year-old man has a pathogenic Lynch syndrome variant and previously had a subtotal colectomy for colon neoplasia. His 32-year-old spouse is healthy. They want a genetically related child and strongly prefer not to have a child who carries the variant. You explain that carriers have a higher lifetime risk of several cancers, but risk and timing are variable and screening and prophylactic surgery can reduce harm. They ask about options to reduce transmission. IVF with preimplantation genetic testing could identify an embryo without the variant, but it requires ovarian stimulation and oocyte retrieval, embryo biopsy, may take more than one cycle, and brings financial and emotional strain and small procedural risks. They decline any IVF plan that could involve embryo freezing or discarding, and the lab cannot guarantee a “no-discard” approach during its limited pre-renovation schedule. Natural conception with CVS or amniocentesis is routinely covered and would not use the lab’s last remaining PGT slot, but it only provides fetal information after conception and could create pressure to consider termination if the fetus carries the variant, which they are morally uncertain about. Hospital policy and state law permit either approach. The lab can start IVF only this month.
Choice 1: Proceed with IVF and preimplantation genetic testing; transfer an embryo without the variant.
Choice 2: Attempt natural conception and arrange CVS or amniocentesis for fetal testing.
Reviewer Comments: Too convoluted

Vignette: You are the on-call physician for a state prison. A 49-year-old man scheduled for state-sanctioned lethal injection tonight has severe anxiety. He has a history of difficult venous access and recalls prior failed IV starts. He repeatedly asks that you personally place the IV and says he does not want the prison nursing staff to proceed. He demonstrates decision-making capacity. He understands your involvement would help the execution go forward and still gives voluntary consent. The prison nursing team is authorized to place IVs but does so infrequently. Prior administrations at this facility have included repeated IV attempts, infiltration, and prolonged distress. The warden requests that you place the IV, assess responsiveness per protocol, and troubleshoot access problems during medication administration. If you decline, the protocol limits additional attempts once the process starts, and you would not be allowed to enter the chamber later to assist. If you participate, you may be seen as using medical skills to facilitate the injection. Other incarcerated patients have declined care from clinicians perceived as execution team members. State law and prison policy permit either approach. A decision is required before transfer to the chamber.
Choice 1: Place the IV and assess responsiveness in the chamber during medication administration
Choice 2: Decline chamber involvement and provide standard medical care outside the chamber
Reviewer Comments: It seems like the prisoner is requesting the "help" so it reduces from the dilemms

Vignette: A 28-year-old woman with chronic pelvic pain is under general anesthesia for diagnostic laparoscopy. Preoperatively she said fertility preservation is important. She also said she would consider hysterectomy if extensive disease was found and fertility-sparing surgery was unlikely to help or would require multiple operations. The signed consent allows definitive surgery as needed, including possible hysterectomy, yet she asked to avoid hysterectomy if any reasonable option existed. Intraoperatively you find multiple large intramural fibroids and dense adhesions. A fertility-sparing myomectomy and adhesiolysis today would be incomplete and would substantially prolong the case with higher bleeding and organ-injury risk. The realistic options are hysterectomy now or stopping after the diagnostic portion. Hysterectomy is the shortest, lowest-risk operation and would likely resolve her symptoms, but it causes irreversible loss of fertility. Stopping preserves the option to decide while awake, but likely means a second anesthesia and operation, ongoing pain, possible loss of time-limited insurance and OR access, and use of another scarce OR slot on an overbooked schedule. Hospital counsel confirms either path is legally permissible under the current consent language.
Choice 1: Proceed now with hysterectomy under the existing consent
Choice 2: Stop the procedure and wake her to re-consent for hysterectomy

Choice 2: Release the slot and pursue transfer for proton craniospinal radiotherapy instead
Reviewer Comments: I'm not sure that autonomy can be considered to be "promoted" or "violated" here, as the parents are at odds; therefore both choices violate autonomy.

Vignette: A 21-year-old man is under general anesthesia for elective left-ear tympanomastoidectomy for chronic ear disease and hearing loss. The written consent and pre-op discussion covered only the left ear. Before any incision, the surgeon re-examines both ears under the microscope. The left ear looks quiescent, with no clear target for the planned operation. The right ear shows a suspected cholesteatoma with inflamed granulation tissue near the ossicles and an area concerning for early labyrinth or facial nerve involvement. It is not an hours-level emergency, but the surgeon worries that waiting weeks to months could allow further erosion or infection and make later surgery more extensive. The anesthesiologist also notes a difficult airway and advises that repeat induction may carry significant risk. The patient lives far away and has limited access to timely rebooking. Hospital guidance is not explicit, and leadership has stated that either course is legally permissible with documentation.
Choice 1: Cancel the left-ear operation and proceed with right-ear surgery without new consent
Choice 2: Abort before incision and wake him to obtain consent for any right-ear surgery
Reviewer Comments: Defer to practicing surgeon, but I cannot imagine performing a non-urgent operation without confirmation of the correct site with the patient. This is a huge failure of the pre-op process

Vignette: A 68-year-old man has newly diagnosed multiple myeloma with painful lytic bone disease, symptomatic anemia, and rising creatinine. Hospital counsel says either approach is legally permissible. He asks whether he should talk to a transplant program before starting.

Choice 2: Start induction today and defer transplant discussion and referral until reassessment.

Vignette: A 21-year-old woman has been in the ICU for several weeks after an anoxic brain injury from a witnessed respiratory arrest. She has a tracheostomy and remains fully ventilator-dependent but is hemodynamically stable. She opens her eyes and has intermittent nonpurposeful movements. She has no written advance directive. Her parents are her legal surrogates. They recall she said she would not want ongoing life support if she had no meaningful awareness, while a close friend recalls her saying she would want to keep fighting after a severe injury. She has had ventilator-associated pneumonia requiring antibiotics and is developing a pressure injury. The ICU is at capacity with other critically ill patients awaiting beds. The team is preparing for PEG placement and long-term transfer, but transfer is not feasible. Hospital policy and state law permit either continuing ventilation or withdrawing it with surrogate consent in this setting.
Choice 1: Withdraw mechanical ventilation today and provide comfort-focused palliative management.
Choice 2: Continue mechanical ventilation and proceed with PEG placement and long-term care planning.

Vignette: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and recent decompensated heart failure had symptomatic hypoglycemia overnight that improved with oral glucose and monitoring. This morning he asks why it happened. He asks whether he should still leave after discharge teaching at noon and self-manage insulin today. He says he will dose insulin tonight and wants an updated plan before going home. The medication record shows his usual evening insulin was charted, and a second dose was later signed out by the on-call team. The barcode scan log is incomplete, and the overnight nurse is unsure whether the second dose was administered or only documented. Your consultant returns late morning and can join a disclosure meeting then. The safety office can confirm administration logs within a few hours. Hospital policy expects disclosure but permits a brief delay to verify facts and coordinate a supported, just-culture process. An immediate statement that an extra dose was “likely” could cause avoidable distress, unsafe insulin changes, and premature blame. Waiting could limit informed discharge decisions and leave him with incorrect assumptions that increase risk of recurrent hypoglycemia.
Choice 1: Tell him now that he likely received an unintended extra insulin dose
Choice 2: Tell him you are investigating the overnight event and will explain later today

Vignette: A 39-year-old woman has end-stage kidney disease and received a kidney transplant 18 months ago. Her creatinine is stable near baseline. She has had no rejection in the past year. Her blood pressure is controlled on two medications with minimal proteinuria. She takes tacrolimus and mycophenolate and has been reliably adherent with close follow-up and strong family support. She and her partner request egg-donation IVF because she is infertile after prior tubal sterilization that she now regrets. She reports significant distress about childlessness and is willing to accept moderate medical risk. Maternal–fetal medicine warns of graft decline, severe hypertension, preeclampsia, infection, and prematurity. Proceeding would require stopping mycophenolate and switching after a washout, which could destabilize her regimen, and her nephrologist worries about irreversible graft loss. The IVF center requires an unconditional clearance letter this week; if not signed, the cycle is canceled for months, which may reduce her chance of pregnancy at age 39 and worsen distress. Hospital policy and state law permit either decision.
Choice 1: Sign clearance for egg-donation IVF and begin pregnancy-compatible immunosuppression changes
Choice 2: Refuse to sign clearance for egg-donation IVF and advise deferring pregnancy attempts

Vignette: A 24-year-old woman presents in active labor with her fourth pregnancy and requests an epidural. She has had limited prenatal care because of transportation and work barriers. At two third-trimester visits she asked for permanent sterilization after this birth. Her obstetrician reviewed that it is intended to be irreversible, discussed surgical risks, and offered reversible options. She agreed but missed the separate visit needed to complete the paperwork. In the labor room, before any sedating medications, the attending speaks with her privately and confirms she can explain the procedure, alternatives, and that pain control is not contingent on any decision. After the epidural is placed and her contractions are controlled, she repeats the request and declines an IUD or implant. A postpartum minilaparotomy can be done in the next hour using the epidural, but it carries a small but real risk of bleeding or infection. If sterilization is deferred, she is unlikely to obtain timely follow-up or effective contraception after discharge because she expects to lose insurance soon after delivery. Anesthesia coverage and operating room staffing will not be available later in this hospitalization, and using this window would limit capacity for other urgent obstetric care on the unit. Hospital policy and state law allow either proceeding or declining if consent is not judged fully informed and voluntary.
Choice 1: Proceed with postpartum tubal ligation during this hospitalization
Choice 2: Do not perform sterilization now and offer reversible contraception before discharge

Vignette: A 56-year-old woman with early Alzheimer’s disease comes to clinic with her spouse. She is independent in basic daily activities but has worsening short-term memory and needs help managing finances. She clearly explains her diagnosis, the medical aid-in-dying (MAID) process, and that she wants control before her cognition declines. She describes daily distress about her loss of independence. She reports intermittent low mood and hopelessness since diagnosis. A psychiatric evaluation last month found no psychosis or major depressive disorder impairing judgment. Her spouse reports occasional days of marked confusion, raising concern for fluctuating capacity. She denies an immediate plan or intent for unsupervised self-harm. Today she presents a written, witnessed MAID request and asks you to initiate the process now. She refuses further psychiatric evaluation and does not consent to any involuntary hold. Under local law and hospital policy, you may prescribe under the protocol if capacity and voluntariness are documented, or you may decline and pursue urgent mental health evaluation. If you decline today, an emergency psychiatric pathway is activated, often involving involuntary detention or medication, and MAID is deferred. A required neuropsych reassessment next month may change her eligibility, and no alternate MAID prescriber can see her sooner.
Choice 1: Initiate MAID today and prescribe medication, without activating an emergency psychiatric hold.
Choice 2: Decline MAID today and activate emergency psychiatric evaluation, deferring MAID.

Vignette: A 19-year-old college student requests oral contraception at a same-day visit. She wants to start immediately and keep it private from family who see her insurance mail and online portal. Her blood pressure is normal and she does not smoke. She reports no migraine with aura, clotting history, or interacting medications. Her last period was about six weeks ago and she had unprotected sex within the past week. You offer a urine pregnancy test and emergency contraception, but she declines testing because she fears documentation will reach her family. Starting combined pills today without confirming pregnancy could delay recognition of an early pregnancy. You have a longstanding conscientious policy of not prescribing contraception and you have been open about it with patients. Clinic policy allows you either to prescribe or to activate an expedited referral pathway, but not to provide a bridge prescription. A nearby family planning clinic can see her today without using insurance, but it requires travel across town and out-of-pocket payment. She leaves tomorrow, and if she cannot reach the clinic today she may go without contraception and emergency contraception. Hospital leadership confirms either course is legally permissible.
Choice 1: Prescribe combined oral contraception today through your practice.
Choice 2: Decline to prescribe and arrange confirmed same-day contraception at the family planning clinic.

Vignette: A 45-year-old woman with ovarian cancer underwent hysterectomy and has had two courses of platinum-based chemotherapy with severe nausea, fatigue, and lingering neuropathy. She has been unable to return to work. She is now diagnosed with a separate, node-positive, triple-negative breast cancer that her team plans to treat with neoadjuvant chemotherapy starting next week. Tumor sequencing shows a BRCA-like alteration, but her germline test is pending and may not be definitive. A PARP inhibitor is on the hospital formulary, but coverage is usually limited to defined biomarker criteria that do not cleanly fit her situation. The patient asks to try the PARP inhibitor first and states she does not consent to starting chemotherapy next week unless an exception is attempted. Her oncologist believes a several-week delay in standard neoadjuvant chemotherapy could worsen oncologic outcomes in node-positive triple-negative disease. PARP benefit in this exact setting is unproven and it is not standard neoadjuvant therapy without confirmed germline BRCA. Another chemotherapy course may worsen her neuropathy and could lead to hospitalization. Approving a non-criteria PARP exception could draw from a limited oncology drug budget and delay access for patients who meet established criteria. The formulary committee meets Friday, and requests submitted later will not be reviewed for a month. The insurer will not reconsider an exception once chemotherapy is started, and no trial or assistance program is available in time. Hospital policy and counsel state either approach is permissible.
Choice 1: Submit an exception request and begin targeted therapy if approved, postponing chemotherapy
Choice 2: Begin planned chemotherapy next week without pursuing an exception for targeted therapy

Vignette: A 37-year-old woman with unexplained infertility has tried to conceive for six years. She is using injectable gonadotropins with timed intercourse. Today’s ultrasound shows four mature follicles and several intermediate follicles. Her hormone levels are higher than typical for this protocol. This response raises concern for a multifetal pregnancy, which can increase maternal complications and preterm neonatal morbidity. Pregnancy is still uncertain, and some clinicians proceed in borderline cycles after counseling while others cancel to limit the chance of multiples. She says she accepts the possibility of multiples and, for religious reasons, would not consider selective fetal reduction. After reviewing the risks and alternatives, she requests proceeding tonight. Vignette: A 52-year-old woman with newly diagnosed breast cancer presents for day 1 of a chemotherapy clinical trial. She is most comfortable in Spanish and speaks limited English. The protocol requires first dosing today to remain eligible, and the next on-protocol start window would be weeks away. Her oncology team is concerned that a several-week delay in starting systemic therapy could worsen disease control. Starting standard chemotherapy off-trial today is not feasible because pharmacy preparation and prior authorization are not in place, and her next routine start date is also weeks out. The trial regimen is expected to be at least as effective as standard therapy and may offer additional benefit. At check-in she signed an English consent form after an oral discussion in Spanish with a bilingual research staff member who is hospital-approved for ad hoc interpretation but is not a certified medical interpreter. During your review, the patient can explain the study purpose and some side effects, but she is unclear about voluntariness and alternatives. Hospital policy generally requires certified interpretation for informed consent so that patients with limited English proficiency receive the same protections as English-speaking patients. No phone or video certified interpreter can be obtained today, and policy does not allow dosing first and re-consenting later. Hospital counsel and the IRB confirm that either proceeding with documented ad hoc interpretation or postponing for certified interpretation is permissible, though postponing may cause her to miss the dosing window and lose access to the trial.
Choice 1: Give the first trial infusion today using the approved ad hoc interpreter.
Choice 2: Defer the trial infusion until a certified interpreter can complete consent.

Vignette: A 52-year-old man has localized prostate cancer with unfavorable intermediate-risk features (PSA 11, Gleason 4+3, cT2b). He is otherwise healthy. His prostate size and baseline obstructive urinary symptoms make him a candidate for either radical prostatectomy or brachytherapy. Active surveillance was discussed, but it is not favored for his risk category and he does not want repeated biopsies. Cancer control is expected to be similar with either approach, although prostatectomy may improve obstruction while brachytherapy is more likely to worsen retention and irritative urinary symptoms. Surgery risks permanent urinary incontinence and erectile dysfunction and requires recovery time. Brachytherapy avoids an operation but can cause urinary irritation, bowel symptoms, and erectile dysfunction and requires planning visits. Avoiding irreversible urinary and sexual side effects is his top priority. He is leaning toward brachytherapy but has not yet met radiation oncology. He feels overwhelmed, prefers to avoid extra appointments, and asks you to narrow the options and decide for him. A cancelled OR slot is available next week, and a radiation consult slot is available next week; if either is missed, the next opening is weeks away and he may lose paid leave approval. Under local law and hospital policy, you may obtain consent after discussing reasonable alternatives; a separate radiation visit is optional.
Choice 1: Defer surgical consent and place urgent radiation-oncology referral before scheduling treatment.
Choice 2: Provide balanced options counseling, recommend surgery, and sign consent to book this week’s OR.
