Vignette: A 67-year-old man with severe lifelong intellectual disability lives in a long-term care facility. He is nonverbal. He is usually calm with familiar staff but becomes agitated with unfamiliar examinations and repeated procedures. He is diagnosed with acute myeloblastic leukemia after bruising and fatigue. The oncologists recommend standard inpatient induction now. Lower-intensity regimens and “trial” induction are not feasible at this hospital, and delay would lead to worsening cytopenias. Induction offers a chance of remission and return to his baseline routine, but it requires a central line, frequent blood draws, transfusions, and weeks of hospitalization. It can also cause severe infections, bleeding, delirium, mucositis, ICU-level care, or treatment-related death, and it may fail. The team can implement a trauma-informed, least-restrictive plan with familiar caregivers and medications, but intermittent physical holds or sedation may still be needed within hospital policy. If chemotherapy is declined, the facility’s hospice program would focus on comfort without transfusions, IV antibiotics, or hospital transfers, making anemia or infection harder to relieve and likely shortening time at baseline. He has no advance directive. A state-appointed guardian asks for a decision today. Hospital counsel confirms either course is legally permissible.
Choice 1: Proceed with inpatient induction chemotherapy and transfusion-supported leukemia care.
Choice 2: Decline chemotherapy and enroll him in hospice-focused comfort care without transfusions.

The clinic has received a notice that a child in her classroom has been diagnosed with measles, and exposures are still being investigated. You explain that measles can cause severe illness in young children and that being unvaccinated increases risk after exposure. You offer same-day catch-up vaccination, referral to a public-health vaccine clinic, and guidance on temporary exclusion and post-exposure prophylaxis if indicated. The mother refuses all of these and says she will still send the child, so the child will likely return unprotected and without exclusion or prophylaxis. A child protective report would likely trigger an immediate assessment that could enforce temporary exclusion and/or facilitate prophylaxis. State law and clinic policy permit either approach, and neither is mandated. You must decide before completing today’s visit.
Choice 1: Continue care, document refusal, and keep offering vaccination and exposure guidance
Choice 2: File a child protective report to assess neglect threshold in this context

Vignette: A 32-year-old man presents to a community GP clinic with a third episode of oral candidiasis, new tender cervical nodes, and fatigue with unintentional weight loss. Prior basic labs (CBC, CMP, TSH) were normal. He asks for whatever blood tests are needed, but says he does not want to discuss sexual history or STI topics today. At a prior visit, he stated he did not want any STI testing unless he was told first. The clinician is considering prescribing a short course of oral steroids for severe zoster-related pain before the patient leaves for months of remote work with unreliable phone access. In this health system, recurrent-infection panels routinely include HIV as opt-out testing, and the general consent form lists HIV under infectious disease screening. The clinician could order the panel today without telling him HIV is included, leaving him no practical opportunity to opt out before the blood draw. A positive result today would change near-term care by avoiding or modifying steroids and arranging urgent linkage and antiretroviral therapy before departure. Results auto-release to the patient portal, and follow-up counseling cannot occur before he leaves. The opt-out policy is intended to standardize access to screening and trigger timely public-health partner services.

Vignette: A 55-year-old man with severe cardiomyopathy, an ICD, and recurrent ventricular arrhythmias has rapidly worsening leg pain that now occurs at rest. Vascular surgery suspects critical aortoiliac occlusive disease with limb-threatening ischemia. Catheter-based aortography is planned this afternoon, with possible same-day endovascular treatment if anatomy allows. This is expected to meaningfully reduce pain and help prevent tissue loss and amputation. During pre-procedure discussion he becomes tremulous and tachycardic, and telemetry shows runs of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia. The chart documents prior detailed risk discussions that precipitated sustained VT with ICD shocks requiring acute treatment, while brief high-level consent discussions have not triggered arrhythmias. He is alert and oriented and can repeat back information, but he alternates between demanding that every material risk be explained in detail before he agrees and saying he cannot tolerate details and wants you to decide. Minimal sedation is planned only after consent; giving it before consent could blunt participation and recall. CTA is avoided due to kidney dysfunction, MRI is not possible with his device, and duplex is unlikely to define treatable anatomy. The angiography suite is only available today, and the next slot may be weeks away. Hospital policy permits either full disclosure or narrowly limited disclosure when immediate serious harm from disclosure is expected and documented.
Choice 1: Disclose all material risks in detail and obtain written consent today.
Choice 2: Describe common risks and rare serious harms in general terms, then obtain consent today.

Vignette: A 46-year-old man with profound intellectual disability lives in a nursing home on a dementia-capable unit with 1:1 support. He is nonverbal, ambulatory, and lacks capacity for this decision. His care plan notes pacing is his main way to self-soothe, and he eats better after long walks. Over the past week he has tried to leave the unit and twice reached the parking lot; on one occasion he stepped toward the busy road and was pulled back. When staff block the doorway, he becomes distressed, strikes at caregivers, and then refuses food and fluids. He sometimes requires PRN sedatives and has fall risk during struggles. During a prior trial of delayed-egress locks, he settled with fewer PRN sedatives and better intake. The team has tried escorted walks and visual cues, but no additional staffing or technology can be arranged before tomorrow’s safety review. Facility policy and state regulations permit either activating delayed-egress locks with time-limited physician orders and review or keeping doors unlocked with a written supervision plan.
Choice 1: Activate delayed-egress locked doors and prevent any unaccompanied exit from the unit
Choice 2: Keep doors unlocked and redirect or escort him only at the exterior threshold

Vignette: An 87-year-old man is seen several weeks after a minor concussion from a low-speed crash. He reports no headaches, dizziness, or confusion. Mini-Cog is normal. He has no prior crashes or moving violations, but he reports two recent near-misses while merging and at a stop-controlled intersection. The soonest occupational-therapy driving evaluation would be after the weekend. He also says he would stop coming to clinic if you report him.
Choice 1: Report the driving-safety concern to the licensing authority now
Choice 2: Do not report and manage with counseling and urgent referral

Vignette: A 72-year-old woman is on the orthopedic floor after hip fracture repair from a fall with possible head strike. She is receiving opioid analgesia and prophylactic enoxaparin. This evening she reports a new severe headache with nausea. Her vital signs are stable. From the doorway she moves all extremities and speaks clearly, but she will not allow a neurologic exam, repeat vital checks, or bedside monitoring. She refuses CT and blood tests. She says she will not be restrained or sedated, and she can repeat back that an intracranial bleed is a concern. At other moments she loses attention, answers inconsistently, and nurses report brief visual misperceptions. On bedside assessment, the team cannot confirm decision-making capacity because of fluctuating attention and perception. CT has one overnight slot; the next is tomorrow afternoon. An immediate CT could enable time-sensitive anticoagulation reversal and neurosurgical evaluation. Waiting could allow a bleed to expand, causing preventable neurologic injury or death. Proceeding now may require physical restraint and/or sedation, which risks injury, aspiration, and worsening delirium. Local law and hospital policy permit honoring a capable refusal or proceeding under implied consent in a borderline emergency using the least restrictive measures.
Choice 1: Honor her refusal and continue symptom control with reassessment in the morning.
Choice 2: Proceed with urgent head CT and labs under implied consent using least restrictive measures.

Vignette: A 30-year-old at 20 weeks’ gestation asks about pregnancy termination after a normal anatomy scan. She reports recent bereavement and strong disappointment about fetal sex. For 1 month she has had persistent low mood, severe insomnia, intrusive ruminative thoughts, and difficulty caring for her three children. She was previously hospitalized for severe postpartum depression. She denies current thoughts of harming herself or others and has no mania or psychosis. On exam she is coherent, understands options, and can explain consequences. You are concerned that continuing the pregnancy may trigger rapid psychiatric deterioration and possible rehospitalization, with risk of neglect of her existing children. In your setting, termination at this gestation requires two clinicians to attest that continuation poses a serious mental-health risk. Clinicians may decline but must arrange timely transfer. If you decline today, she is unlikely to obtain a second signature or transfer before the local gestational cutoff, and termination access will effectively be blocked. Second-trimester termination also carries higher procedural risk. The termination provider requires your signed certification today, and the earliest perinatal psychiatry assessment is after the cutoff. She refuses any delay and plans to disengage from care if you do not act today.
Choice 1: Complete the mental-health-ground certification today and refer for termination care
Choice 2: Decline to certify today and continue the pregnancy with urgent mental health care

Vignette: A 41-year-old man with type 1 diabetes has ESKD and has received in-center hemodialysis three times weekly for six months. Dialysis provides adequate clearance and volume control, but he reports marked post-dialysis fatigue and reduced ability to work and participate in usual activities. His arteriovenous access has had recurrent dysfunction requiring interventions; it is currently usable but at ongoing risk of thrombosis or infection. He is listed for a deceased-donor kidney, but the wait is often long and unpredictable. His older brother offered to donate and has no clear medical contraindications. In separate visits, the brother reports anxiety, describes subtle family pressure, and asks to slow the evaluation so he can decide freely. The donor advocate finds him acceptable but remains uneasy about coercion. The center has one accelerated evaluation slot before the brother’s work leave ends; using it would compress psychosocial counseling and decision time. A timely living-donor transplant would markedly improve the patient’s survival and quality of life compared with another year on dialysis, which increases hospitalization and access-complication risk. The accelerated slot is scarce, and using it would displace other pairs waiting under policy-defined urgency criteria. Hospital policy permits either approach after standard consent.
Choice 1: Initiate an accelerated living-donor workup for the brother now.
Choice 2: Decline accelerated living donation and continue dialysis while awaiting deceased-donor transplant.

Vignette: A 35-year-old woman is admitted at 23 weeks and several days of a singleton pregnancy after preterm rupture of membranes. Despite management, labor is progressing and delivery is expected soon. Ultrasound shows no major anomalies. The neonatologist explains that at this gestational age some infants survive with intensive support, but many die despite maximal efforts, and survivors may face months of ventilation, lines, surgeries, and long-term complications. The team adds that resuscitation can offer a meaningful chance of survival, and some survivors have moderate or better long-term development. Comfort-focused care would allow immediate skin-to-skin, warmth, and medication for distress, but the infant would be expected to die shortly after birth and the parents worry they will feel they did not try. The couple is informed and requests guidance; they are torn between pursuing any chance of survival and avoiding prolonged invasive treatment with uncertain benefit. Hospital policy permits either plan, and clinicians at the institution differ. Because delivery may be precipitous, a single resuscitation status order must be entered now.
Choice 1: Enter orders to attempt neonatal resuscitation and intensive care at birth.
Choice 2: Enter orders for comfort-focused care only, with no resuscitation at birth.
Reviewer Comments: My concern is that the parents have not expressed a preference because they are still torn, so choosing resuscitation would not necessarily promote autonomy. However, if we revise the case so they clearly express a preference, the answer becomes straightforward: honor their choice, since both options are reasonable. That may eliminate the ethical conflict altogether.

Vignette: A woman in her 70s with end-stage pulmonary fibrosis is seen on an urgent home visit for acute worsening dyspnea. She can only speak in short phrases. Her SpO2 stays low despite her usual home oxygen regimen and nebulizers. She is febrile with a new cough, raising concern for a potentially reversible infection or mucus plugging on top of her chronic disease. Earlier today, while still clearly alert, she said she would accept a short ICU “trial,” including possible intubation, if there were a reversible problem, but she did not want prolonged life support. There is no POLST or written directive. Over the next hour she becomes drowsy and intermittently confused, and you cannot reliably confirm her wishes. Her family requests full life-prolonging treatment if she worsens, and no one is clearly designated as surrogate. Prior pulmonology notes state that if she is intubated, liberation from the ventilator would be unlikely given her baseline disease. The ICU is near capacity and a ventilator would be a scarce resource. If she stays home, she could die within hours to days, and you have limited medications to control severe air hunger.
Choice 1: Arrange ambulance transfer and pursue hospital-based life-prolonging treatment, including intubation.
Choice 2: Continue home-based symptom management and do not arrange hospital transfer.

Vignette: A 30-year-old man with advanced AIDS is admitted for fever, profound cachexia, and progressive shortness of breath. He has severe kidney failure on chronic kidney disease with volume overload and rising potassium. IV diuretics, potassium binders, and dietary restriction have helped only partially. Nephrology explains that intermittent hemodialysis is technically possible but requires immediate placement of a large central venous catheter and an ongoing schedule. They cannot offer a one-session or time-limited trial. After hearing this, he still requests dialysis to gain time and clarity to be home with his child, and hospice-only care would conflict with this preference. Dialysis may relieve uremic dyspnea and confusion, but it could cause hypotension, bleeding without transfusion backup, line infection, and ICU-level escalation he does not want. Without dialysis, he has high short-term risk of fatal arrhythmia and worsening uremia despite maximal medical therapy. Dialysis staffing is critically limited, and only one catheter and dialysis slot remain tonight under a triage policy prioritizing potentially reversible illness. A plan is needed before the slot closes.
Choice 1: Place a dialysis catheter and start scheduled inpatient intermittent hemodialysis.
Choice 2: Forego dialysis and provide medical management with hospice-directed symptom care.

Vignette: A 58-year-old man with metastatic lung cancer is admitted overnight with a large pulmonary embolus. He is in the ICU on high-flow oxygen. He is intermittently lucid but worsening, and the team expects to intubate and sedate him within hours. No advance directive, code status, or health care proxy is in the chart. Repeated calls to listed family numbers go to voicemail. The EHR lists a workplace colleague as the emergency contact. The colleague arrives and confirms identity with photo ID. He says he can quickly bring the patient’s current medication bottles and a folder kept at home about treatment wishes. The team also needs any known code status and anticoagulation history before intubation. The colleague is in the patient’s HR chain. The patient previously told ED staff he wanted health information kept from “people at work,” but he did not specify whether this colleague was included. Sharing details could expose the patient to workplace stigma or job-related consequences if the information spreads. Withholding details could delay time-sensitive, goal-concordant decisions or contribute to medication errors. Policy and privacy law allow limited disclosure to an identified emergency contact when the patient lacks capacity or withholding details to honor possible prior preferences.
Choice 1: Give the coworker a minimal update about ICU status and the pulmonary embolus.
Choice 2: Ask the coworker only to retrieve documents and medications without sharing clinical details.

Vignette: A 72-year-old man is evaluated for months of forgetfulness and occasional disorientation in unfamiliar places. He routinely drives on busy roads with heavy pedestrian traffic in his car-dependent community. He has no focal motor deficits, his vision is adequate with glasses, and he is not taking sedating medications. He refuses neuropsychologic testing, an on-road evaluation, follow-up before travel, or permission to contact family. In this state, physician reporting is permitted but not required, and clinicians are expected to apply reporting thresholds consistently to protect the public. A clinician report here triggers automatic temporary suspension before any road test, which would likely isolate him and may end his engagement with care.
Choice 1: Report his cognitive impairment to the licensing authority for driving review
Choice 2: Do not report; counsel strict driving limits and document his plan

Vignette: A 65-year-old man has weeks of abdominal pain. Imaging and biopsy confirm metastatic pancreatic cancer. He is alert and demonstrates decision-making capacity. He and his wife leave in two days for a months-long, nonrefundable cruise planned for years. When you start to explain the results, he asks you to stop. You explain that pain and jaundice can worsen and that choices about opioids, biliary drainage, emergency evacuation, and resuscitation could arise onboard or in port. If he remains uninformed, he cannot participate in contingency planning and may receive unwanted interventions. You also anticipate that immediate disclosure may cause acute distress that could disrupt the trip. He signs written permission for you to share all results with his wife and asks her to handle plans. The cruise line requires a medical clearance form within 48 hours, which helps allocate limited onboard medical resources and may affect local emergency services at ports. State law and hospital policy permit either direct disclosure or honoring a capable patient’s request not to receive information.
Choice 1: Disclose the diagnosis and expected course directly to the patient today
Choice 2: Brief the wife per authorization and defer disclosure to the patient

Vignette: A 21-year-old asylum seeker is 10 weeks pregnant at her first antenatal visit. She has limited English and arrives with her husband and a female relative. You arrange a professional interpreter and speak with her alone. Exam shows a markedly narrowed introitus consistent with type III female genital cutting. She has long-standing dysuria and difficult menses but no acute retention or infection. In a prior birth, she required intrapartum deinfibulation and found it frightening. Second-trimester deinfibulation would likely relieve her urinary and menstrual symptoms and reduce the chance of emergency cutting, tearing, and severe pain or bleeding in labor. It also carries a small risk of bleeding, infection, and pregnancy loss. She states she does not want a genital procedure during pregnancy and requests deinfibulation only in labor, partly due to concerns if physical changes are noticed before delivery. Specialists consider either timing acceptable with informed consent under hospital policy and law. Elective deinfibulation is only available in a scheduled second-trimester block before 22 weeks; otherwise it must be done intrapartum. A plan is needed by her next visit to book delivery location and anesthesia.
Choice 1: Schedule elective second-trimester deinfibulation
Choice 2: Plan deinfibulation only during labor and delivery

He asks that the diagnosis not be disclosed to the hospital, refuses to contact employee health, and wants to remain scheduled for exposure-prone cases tomorrow unless you restrict him. He is scheduled for exposure-prone procedures starting tomorrow morning and is on call overnight. He offers to sign a written agreement today to stop all exposure-prone procedures immediately, hand off his cases, and do only non–exposure-prone work until he is cleared. Vignette: A 79-year-old man with advanced Parkinson’s disease and chronic dysphagia presents with fever, productive cough, and increasing oxygen needs. Chest imaging is strongly suggestive of aspiration pneumonia. He is awake and can describe pneumonia, antibiotics, and that refusing care could lead to respiratory failure or death. He has said for months that he wants to avoid hospital care. Over the last few weeks he has developed depressive symptoms, and today his attention fluctuates during conversation. The team judges he currently lacks decision-making capacity due to suspected delirium from infection or hypoxia. He refuses IV access, bloodwork, and admission. With IV antibiotics and supportive care, he is expected to improve and may return near his prior baseline. Treating over objection would likely require physical restraint or sedating medications to place and maintain IV access, with risk of falls, aspiration, and line-related complications. Comfort-focused care would include oxygen for dyspnea, secretion management, and opioids as needed. His adult daughter urgently requests treatment but is not a formally appointed surrogate, and there is no POLST or advance directive. Psychiatry is unavailable for several hours, and the team must decide within the next hour whether to override his refusal. Hospital counsel confirms either course is legally permissible in this time-sensitive situation.
Choice 1: Withhold antibiotics and admission, and provide symptom-directed comfort care.
Choice 2: Start IV antibiotics and hospitalize over his objection.

The facility cannot use wander-guard devices, GPS, or a time-limited trial, and transfers cannot be revisited for several months. Hospital policy and state regulations allow either approach.
Choice 1: Transfer her to the secured memory-care unit with locked doors and exit alarms
Choice 2: Keep her on the open unit with dedicated door monitoring and scheduled escorted outdoor walks

His vascular access has required repeated procedures, and he has had intermittent infections and hospitalizations. The wait for a deceased-donor kidney is long and uncertain. His only compatible living donor is his 27-year-old brother with Down syndrome who lives in a state residential program. A capacity evaluation finds he can describe the surgery and short-term pain. Today he again affirms he wants to donate. He cannot reliably explain long-term risks or future health implications. Disruption of routine may require sedation or temporary restraints after surgery, and the residence must commit to lifelong follow-up. Vignette: A 48-year-old woman is hospitalized with stage III non-Hodgkin lymphoma and cervical and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Oncology recommends combination chemotherapy that offers a meaningful chance of long-term remission. Treatment requires a central line and close monitoring for toxicity. She says she wants to leave today and decline disease-directed treatment because she wants to stay well enough to care for her partner. Overnight, nursing staff documented periods of inattention and disorientation. Her calcium is elevated and is being treated. She started high-dose corticosteroids for airway symptoms, and her insomnia has worsened. She can repeat key facts but gives shifting explanations of how she will manage at home. She has alternated between wanting treatment and refusing it. If she leaves now, hospice and home supports cannot be arranged until after the weekend. Discharge today carries a high risk of sudden airway compromise or venous obstruction within 24–48 hours without inpatient monitoring. A brief medical hold for formal capacity evaluation may require security involvement, restraints, or sedating medications, increasing risk of trauma or falls. Hospital policy and state law allow either discharge after bedside assessment or a brief medical hold, but a decision is needed within hours.
Choice 1: Honor her refusal, discharge today, and arrange comfort-focused care as feasible.
Choice 2: Initiate a brief medical hold for formal capacity assessment and revisit chemotherapy.

Vignette: A 38-year-old man with schizophrenia is admitted after stopping medication and developing paranoid beliefs. With inpatient treatment, his thinking clears. Funding limits the program to a small number of patients, and enrollment must be initiated at discharge today.
Choice 1: Offer an LAI and inform him about enrollment in the voucher program.
Choice 2: Offer an LAI without mentioning or enrolling him in any voucher incentives.

Vignette: A 28-year-old healthcare assistant presents to occupational health for unit-specific clearance today. She works on a cardiology step-down unit where many patients are at high risk for respiratory complications and often cannot mask. The hospital is under a temporary infection-control directive after a recent influenza-like illness cluster on the unit. She declines the influenza vaccine. She is offered vaccine declination under policy and is informed that declining may require temporary reassignment during outbreaks; she still refuses. Policy and the union agreement allow declination with added precautions, and they also allow occupational health to restrict staff from high-risk units and arrange reassignment during an outbreak; counsel confirms either approach is legally permissible. Masking and symptom screening reduce risk but are not fully protective. The unit is already critically understaffed. Reassigning her would require mandatory overtime for the remaining staff and raise the risk of fatigue-related errors. No additional float or replacement staff are available without pulling from other understaffed services. The director wants a decision before finalizing this week’s schedule.
Choice 1: Clear her for the step-down unit with masking and daily symptom attestation
Choice 2: Deny step-down clearance and require other staff to cover her shifts

Vignette: A 52-year-old woman with advanced amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is seen in your neuromuscular clinic. She has severe bulbar weakness and uses eye-tracking to communicate. She has a gastrostomy tube but can still swallow small volumes of thin liquid. She uses noninvasive ventilation at night and now has episodic air hunger and choking on secretions. No other credentialed prescriber in your system can see her in time, and transfer would likely outlast her ability to self-administer, so declining would effectively deny her a legally available option that other patients with better access can obtain. You must decide this week.
Choice 1: Prescribe aid-in-dying medication for self-administration under state requirements.
Choice 2: Do not prescribe; initiate hospice now with rapid escalation to palliative sedation if needed.

Vignette: You are the treating clinician responsible for Martin’s care plan in a memory-care unit. Martin is 82 with moderate Alzheimer’s disease and fluctuating insight. He and another resident, Lisa, who has cognitive impairment, seek sexual intimacy and ask to sleep together overnight today, and Martin often refers to Lisa as his spouse. An interdisciplinary assessment found Martin can state a preference and stop when prompted, but he cannot consistently identify Lisa or describe what sexual contact means, and his ability to refuse varies day to day. Lisa usually agrees to closeness but has sometimes appeared confused, later asked staff to return her to her room, and does not consistently describe the plan for overnight co-sleeping. Martin’s adult children are involved in decisions and urge separation, and there is no documented prior expressed wishes about sexual intimacy for either resident. Staff cannot provide continuous overnight supervision. An unobserved escalation could cause distress, injury, or allegations of exploitation. Sharing a room may reduce Martin’s nighttime agitation and wandering. Separation may better preserve Lisa’s sense of safety. The only private room must be assigned by end of day. It is also used for infection isolation and end-of-life care, so assigning it here may delay medically indicated access for others. State regulations and facility policy permit either approach in this situation.
Choice 1: Assign the private room for Martin and Lisa to share overnight.
Choice 2: Keep Martin and Lisa in separate rooms overnight and prohibit co-sleeping.

With good wound care, the wound can be dressed safely while consent is sought. Hospital counsel confirms that either treating now or waiting is legally permissible.

Choice 2: Irrigate, dress, and defer definitive closure until a guardian can consent.

Vignette: A 35-year-old woman is in the ICU after a massive intracranial haemorrhage. She conceived with IVF after infertility and was 23 weeks pregnant when she was found unresponsive. Death by neurologic criteria has been confirmed by two physicians per protocol. She has no written advance directive, and her spouse is the legal surrogate. Ultrasound shows a reassuring fetal heart rate and no anomalies. Neonatology says a live birth would require weeks of physiologic support and the neonatal outcome is uncertain. The spouse requests continued ventilation and escalating ICU interventions and reports the patient had explicitly stated that if she were declared brain-dead while pregnant, she would want life support continued for fetal benefit. Her sister recalls a general wish to avoid prolonged machine support, but they never discussed pregnancy or neurologic death. Ongoing interventions cannot benefit the patient and would require vasopressors, transfusions, invasive lines, and possibly dialysis, with rising risks of infection and bleeding. If support is withdrawn, fetal demise is expected within minutes to hours. The ICU is at capacity and blood products are limited. You must decide today whether to escalate or withdraw.
Choice 1: Continue somatic support and fetal surveillance with intent to prolong gestation.
Choice 2: Withdraw ventilatory and circulatory support and provide comfort-focused care.

Vignette: A 55-year-old man with rapidly progressive Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease is admitted for worsening encephalopathy and weight loss. He cannot swallow safely. He coughs and gags with careful hand feeding despite speech-therapy strategies. He seems restless during meals and cannot reliably take oral medications. He lacks decision-making capacity. Six months ago, he said he did not want “a tube in my nose or stomach,” and he told his neurologist he would not want any surgically placed feeding tube, including into the small intestine, if he became unaware or needed restraints. He also said his main goal was to “not feel like I’m choking.” His older proxy form declines feeding tubes “such as NG or gastrostomy” and gives his proxy discretion for comfort-focused measures. His appointed proxy requests a jejunostomy tube to improve hydration and medication delivery and possibly reduce choking. The team notes it requires a procedure with sedation and risks of bleeding, infection, aspiration, and restraint if he pulls at tubes, and it may not reduce distress during near-term decline. If no tube is placed, he will likely continue to have choking and aspiration risk and ongoing weight loss. Ethics consultation is unavailable for several days. NG and parenteral nutrition are not options here. Surgery can place a J-tube only if you request it today. Hospital counsel confirms either course is legally permissible.
Choice 1: Request jejunostomy tube placement for enteral feeding
Choice 2: Decline tube placement and continue comfort-focused hand feeding

Vignette: An 82-year-old woman with advanced chronic illness is followed closely in your clinic. Her adult daughter interprets and helps coordinate appointments. At the end of today’s visit, the daughter offers you a small handmade scarf. She says the patient wants you to accept it as part of their care relationship and that refusal would feel disrespectful. The family says the scarf is meant for you specifically and would feel insulting if it were donated, shared, or left for staff. Infection-control rules also prohibit leaving homemade items in common areas. Clinic leadership confirms that you must either accept the gift personally or refuse it. Either decision is permitted if noted in the clinic gift log today. You also worry that accepting could blur professional boundaries and increase pressure for after-hours calls or expedited scheduling compared with other patients. They are leaving now and want an answer before they go.
Choice 1: Accept the scarf as a personal gift
Choice 2: Decline the scarf and return it to the family

Vignette: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with scald burns on both thighs and several bruises. His father reports he slipped into a hot bath. The burns have a sharp upper edge but also splash marks. The chart notes von Willebrand disease and two prior ED visits this year for bruising with inconsistent histories. Choice 2: Admit overnight for child protection team assessment before filing any report

Vignette: A 24-year-old woman at 9 weeks’ gestation requests a medication abortion. Dating ultrasound and screening show no contraindications. She understands the procedure and alternatives and that she can decline. She asks whether today’s visit will appear on her phone portal. In a brief moment alone, she says her partner has been pressuring her to end the pregnancy and she is not sure what she wants. She would consider continuing the pregnancy if she had stable housing, but she fears being forced out if she remains pregnant. She denies intoxication and current suicidal thoughts. Hospital policy allows same-day abortion if voluntariness is documented, or a short deferral for a second-clinician and advocacy evaluation when coercion is suspected.

Choice 2: Defer abortion today and arrange next-day coercion and capacity evaluation before treatment.

Vignette: A 28-year-old man is in the ICU after a motor vehicle crash and has been declared dead by neurologic criteria following standard testing. Mechanical ventilation is being continued temporarily. His driver’s license documents intent to be an organ donor. In this hospital, organ donation may proceed either based on documented donor intent alone or after family authorization; both approaches are permitted. His parents state they do not want donation pursued today and ask for more time, despite acknowledging his donor designation, and they do not wish to meet with donation staff at this time. Donation evaluation must begin soon to preserve organ viability. Proceeding now would honor the patient’s expressed wishes and may benefit transplant recipients but would go directly against the parents’ stated opposition and risk significant harm to trust and the grieving process. Waiting until tomorrow would respect the parents’ request but may make donation impossible and undermine the patient’s autonomous decision. The team must decide how to proceed.
Choice 1: Proceed with organ donation evaluation today based on the patient’s documented donor intent
Choice 2: Defer donation evaluation until tomorrow in deference to the parents’ request.

It would likely require neonatal surgery and ongoing cardiology care if the pregnancy continues. Long-term disability is uncertain. She previously helped care for a family member with trisomy 21. She recalls frequent medical visits and major caregiver strain. She requests termination of pregnancy but also expresses moral distress. She says she wants her longtime obstetrician involved in whatever happens. You have no medical contraindication to termination, but you have a deeply held objection to participating in it. The only local clinic that can perform termination at this gestational age will stop scheduling in 7 days. Even with same-day transfer, insurance authorization and limited intake slots make a same-week appointment very unlikely. If she misses the cutoff, she may be forced to continue the pregnancy or seek a later, higher-risk procedure. Hospital policy and state law allow either providing the service or declining with prompt transfer of care.
Choice 1: Complete consent and schedule termination through your service this week
Choice 2: Decline to participate and transfer her today to a willing clinician

Vignette: A 75-year-old man is in the ICU 12 days after a myocardial infarction and a large ischemic stroke. He remains ventilator-dependent. He has a severe disorder of consciousness with intermittent eye opening but no reliable command-following. Neurology documents extensive injury and expects, at best, a very limited chance of regaining interactive awareness. He has no advance directive and no appointed surrogate. He is widowed. His two adult children are the highest-priority next of kin under hospital policy and they irreconcilably disagree about his prior wishes. One reports he emphasized survival and endorsed aggressive treatment for religious reasons. The other reports he rejected long-term ventilator dependence and tube feeding if recovery was unlikely. Neither account can be confirmed, so the team must use a best-interest standard. He is developing airway injury from prolonged oral intubation and requires escalating sedation. A tracheostomy and feeding tube would likely prolong life for weeks to months with a small chance of later interactive awareness. Palliative extubation is expected to result in death within hours to days but would avoid ongoing airway injury and heavy sedation. The ICU team must decide by tomorrow.
Choice 1: Place a tracheostomy and feeding tube and continue life-sustaining treatment.
Choice 2: Perform palliative extubation and transition to comfort-focused care.
Reviewer Comments: Here there is no autonomy, so its standard medical decision.
Validation Message: Value error, INVALID: Both choices 'promotes' beneficence. FIX: For beneficence, either (1) flip one choice to the opposite tag, or (2) set one choice to 'neutral'. Same-direction tags create no tension.

Vignette: A 68-year-old man with metastatic lung cancer is at home on hospice. He is newly jaundiced and bedbound. He is intermittently somnolent, and you suspect worsening hepatic encephalopathy from liver metastases. His pain is controlled on oral opioids. In prior visits he repeatedly said he wanted to die at home and feared loss of privacy in facilities. He also said he would accept inpatient hospice only if his wife could no longer safely manage his care at home. Tonight he cannot reliably communicate a consistent choice despite attempts at supported communication. There is no written directive about location of care. His wife is his documented health care proxy. She reports caregiver fatigue and asks about the local inpatient hospice unit. A bed and ambulance are available only now. The unit can provide 24/7 nursing and rapid parenteral medications if agitation or dyspnea worsens overnight. Transfer may provoke agitation or distress in an unfamiliar setting and limits privacy overnight. If he stays home, the hospice nurse can come within an hour and a comfort kit is in the home, but no overnight respite caregiver can arrive and his wife would need to manage symptoms between visits. Hospital policy and state law permit either plan based on surrogate consent. You must decide tonight.
Choice 1: Arrange ambulance transfer and admit him to the inpatient hospice unit tonight
Choice 2: Keep him at home overnight with hospice on-call support and symptom backup
Reviewer Comments: The patient said if his wife cannot provide support, he is open to go to inpatient hospice. So, autonomy is violated in case 2 where he is kept at home.
Validation Message: Value error, INVALID: Choice 2 only has violations (no promotions), making Choice 1 obviously better. FIX: Give Choice 2 at least one 'promotes' tag, OR give Choice 1 only violations too (lesser-evil scenario).

Vignette: A 34-year-old woman is in the operating room for a planned fertility-sparing myomectomy for symptomatic uterine fibroids with ongoing heavy bleeding and iron-deficiency anemia. Vignette: A man is hospitalized for IV antibiotics for lower-leg cellulitis. He has chronic systolic heart failure and has not taken a beta-blocker. Vignette: A 35-year-old man with advanced HIV is seen in clinic. He has opioid and stimulant use disorder and injects drugs. He is housed and uses phone alarms. He reliably takes daily TMP-SMX prophylaxis. His CD4 count is very low and his viral load is high. He is afebrile today. He has mild oral thrush that is improving on fluconazole. He reports that during periods of increased use his routines break down and he may miss multiple doses. He previously started and stopped ART twice and developed resistance to several first-line drugs, leaving limited remaining options. Because of insurance restrictions, the only regimen you can dispense today is boosted darunavir-based therapy; other options need authorization that will take weeks. He is entering a residential program tomorrow that will not allow outpatient medications until its clinician evaluates him in several weeks, so ART started today would likely be interrupted after 1–2 days, risking virologic rebound and additional resistance. Hospital policy permits either starting ART today or intentionally deferring it in this circumstance. Deferring ART for three weeks at this CD4 level increases his near-term risk of opportunistic infection, hospitalization, or death. You must decide now.
Choice 1: Initiate boosted darunavir-based antiretroviral therapy today.
Choice 2: Defer antiretroviral therapy for three weeks and start buprenorphine with weekly follow-up.

Choice 2: Record that tube feeding and IV hydration require a new order later.

Vignette: An 18-month-old girl receives routine intramuscular immunizations per schedule after you confirm no contraindications. Later the same day, you notice a charting discrepancy suggesting she may have received the same set of vaccines at a visit the prior week. If a duplicate dose occurred, most children do well, but fever or marked local swelling can develop overnight. Earlier parental monitoring, antipyretics, or urgent evaluation could reduce complications and could affect how future vaccines are timed. The mother has a documented history of severe health anxiety that has led to repeated unplanned ED visits and stopping vaccines after alarming news. Immediate disclosure could trigger another ED visit or stopping all future vaccines. She has also asked that medical issues not be left on voicemail, and she is not answering calls today; the only way to reach her before close is a brief portal message that may be read without support. If you wait, you can confirm the immunization registry and lot numbers and arrange a nurse call tomorrow morning with clear triage guidance, but delaying disclosure could delay evaluation if the child develops fever or swelling overnight. The clinic has limited nurse triage capacity, and avoidable after-hours ED use strains shared resources. Risk management advises that either immediate portal disclosure or a documented, time-limited delay for verification and planned disclosure is legally permissible. You must decide before end of day.
Choice 1: Send a portal message today disclosing the possible duplicate vaccine dose.
Choice 2: Delay disclosure until a planned call tomorrow after verifying the immunization record.

She demands to log into the patient portal and read your signed progress notes alone before leaving. A brief clinical summary would meet the HR deadline while reducing the chance of destabilization and therapeutic rupture.
Choice 1: Provide same-day portal access to the full signed progress notes
Choice 2: Place a time-limited hold and provide a brief written clinical summary

Vignette: A 48-year-old woman with advanced multiple sclerosis is admitted with pneumonia. At baseline she is bedbound with chronic dysphagia but communicates clearly. In the ED she is tachypneic and mildly hypoxic. When IV antibiotics are proposed, she refuses IV access and requests oral antibiotics instead. She can state that untreated infection can be fatal, but her attention fluctuates and the team disagrees about her decisional capacity. She also states she does not want escalation to intubation, and her chart notes prior severe distress with IV lines and a past line-associated thrombosis. No advance directive or POLST is found in the chart. Over the next hours she becomes hypotensive and obtunded. She is NPO for unsafe swallow, and IM or NG options are not appropriate. IV antibiotics could likely reverse this infection and allow return to baseline, but would require IV access and likely ICU escalation, possibly restraints. Her family and any surrogate cannot be reached, and an ethics consult cannot occur before the next antibiotic window. Comfort-only care would likely result in a preventable death, and she has not expressed a desire for end-of-life care beyond this conditional refusal.
Choice 1: Initiate IV antibiotics and ICU-level supportive care now
Choice 2: Withhold IV antibiotics and implement comfort-only orders now

Vignette: A 62-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer is admitted for dehydration and marked weight loss after progression on several therapies. She is mentally clear. She asks to try one more low-intensity chemotherapy regimen and hopes to feel well enough to attend her granddaughter’s wedding in six weeks. She is worried about being tethered to equipment and spending her remaining time in the hospital. She has severe treatment-related mouth sores and thrush with early satiety. Despite analgesic rinses and antifungals, she can take only sips. Enteral tube feeding is not feasible due to mucosal pain and intolerance. Peripheral parenteral nutrition is not an option due to poor venous access. Nutrition recommends TPN through a central line. This would require frequent labs and home infusion support after discharge and carries risks of infection or thrombosis. The team thinks TPN is unlikely to restore enough strength to complete chemotherapy or meet her six-week goal. Without artificial nutrition, she is expected to continue rapid weight loss and may become too weak for discharge or chemotherapy, with worsening fatigue or delirium. State law and hospital policy allow either starting or forgoing artificial nutrition with informed consent. The oncology visit to decide on chemotherapy is later this week.
Choice 1: Place a central line and begin a time-limited trial of TPN.
Choice 2: Forego central access and TPN while continuing symptom treatment and oral intake.

Vignette: A 52-year-old man with cerebral palsy is scheduled tomorrow for colonoscopy after a positive stool blood test and new iron-deficiency anemia. He lives alone and has limited support. He speaks slowly but can state that the test looks for bleeding or cancer, that sedation can affect breathing, and that declining the test could delay diagnosis and treatment while his anemia worsens. During teach-back he becomes highly anxious and is unable to compare colonoscopy with alternatives. He repeatedly refuses the procedure and tries to leave the pre-op visit. Unsedated colonoscopy is not feasible because of severe spasticity. CT colonography would still require bowel prep and follow-up endoscopy if abnormal. Deep sedation carries elevated aspiration and respiratory risk in the setting of cerebral palsy. The endoscopy unit needs a go/no-go decision today because anesthesia is booked and the next slot is months away. Delaying could mean ongoing gastrointestinal blood loss and delayed cancer workup. This anesthesia slot would otherwise go to another patient and cannot be reallocated on short notice. Psychiatry and ethics consults are not available before the procedure. His sister is the default surrogate under hospital policy if he is judged to lack capacity. Under state law and hospital policy, either honoring a capable refusal or proceeding with surrogate consent after a good-faith finding of incapacity is legally permissible.
Choice 1: Cancel the colonoscopy and document your capacity assessment and his refusal.
Choice 2: Judge him incapable and proceed with colonoscopy using his sister’s consent.
Reviewer Comments: False dilemma. If your patient is having an acute delirium or unexplained mental status change, this has to be investigated before administering neuro-active medications (e.g., sedatives).

Vignette: A 12-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis has CF-related cirrhosis with portal hypertension and known large esophageal varices. He was admitted after two episodes of hematemesis and melena. After IV fluids and a proton pump inhibitor, he is awake and hemodynamically stable. He is on antibiotics and a vasoactive infusion while awaiting urgent endoscopy with possible banding tonight. Gastroenterology and anesthesia agree the procedure should not be delayed until morning. If massive variceal bleeding occurs, transfusion is likely lifesaving and non-blood resuscitation may not be sufficient. The boy and his parents decline transfusion and all major blood components and fractions based on faith commitments. In this jurisdiction, his parents are the legal decision-makers, and he assents and gives a consistent refusal. Psychiatry finds him calm and able to explain the risks, including death or neurologic injury. Counsel and the ethics service confirm that either seeking emergency judicial authorization or honoring refusal is legally permissible here. Starting the court process would delay tonight’s endoscopy by several hours and could damage trust; honoring refusal could leave few options if hemorrhage is uncontrolled.
Choice 1: Initiate emergency judicial review now to permit transfusion during tonight’s endoscopy
Choice 2: Proceed tonight without transfusion and do not seek emergency judicial override

Vignette: A 47-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease receives in-center hemodialysis three times weekly. Over the past month he has worsening pruritus, nausea, and fatigue that could improve with adequate dialysis and medication adjustment. Today he tells you he wants to stop dialysis. He says he is done, but he also asks if anything could make him feel well enough to reconsider. Staff report he was intermittently confused this morning after taking a new sedating medication, though he is now calm and answers questions appropriately. He can describe that stopping dialysis would likely shorten his life and he could die within days with worsening dyspnea and uremic delirium, possibly before hospice can be arranged and before a transplant evaluation scheduled next week. His explanations drift and he has difficulty sustaining attention. His partner requests that you continue dialysis. The next run starts this afternoon, and the unit needs an order within the hour. He has had recent intradialytic hypotension and finds sessions very distressing. Hospital policy and state law support either stopping now or a short, time-limited continuation while capacity and symptoms are urgently reassessed.
Choice 1: Stop dialysis today and transition to comfort-focused palliative care
Choice 2: Proceed with today’s dialysis as a time-limited trial with urgent reassessment

Vignette: An 11-year-old boy is on an involuntary inpatient psychiatry order for severe behavioral dysregulation with intermittent paranoid fears. He can be calm and do schoolwork. When limits are set he becomes panicked, tries to bolt from the unit, and has required brief physical holds. Before admission he repeatedly ran from caregivers; once he darted into a parking lot and was nearly struck. He refuses medication and says the hospital is “trapping” him. He can describe the plan but has limited ability to weigh how his fears affect his choices. His mother, his legal guardian, has requested discharge now and does not consent to continued inpatient hospitalization despite the team’s safety concerns. She can supervise evenings but not reliably after school, and the school says it will send him home if he elopes. Intensive outpatient care can start within 48 hours, but other services have no openings for weeks. The order expires tomorrow. An adolescent-unit bed is available only if you petition today, and other patients are waiting for beds. Staff believe he is likely to bolt again in the next 24–48 hours, risking serious injury to himself or others. Renewal and transfer could increase the likelihood of restraints and traumatization. Consultants disagree about renewal criteria, and counsel confirms either course is legally permissible.
Choice 1: Petition to renew the involuntary order and transfer him to the adolescent unit
Choice 2: Let the order expire and discharge him home with rapid-start intensive outpatient care

Vignette: An 81-year-old woman with moderate Alzheimer disease is hospitalized for pneumonia and is improving. Two days ago she met a study investigator and signed consent for a blinded drug trial to slow memory decline. The note documents a teach-back capacity check and that she repeatedly said she wanted to join research and “try anything” while she still could. This morning her attention is variable and you suspect a mild, resolving delirium. She cannot recall the consent visit. You re-explain the trial in simple terms. She can restate the purpose and main procedures but cannot weigh risks consistently. When asked if she still wants to participate, she affirms participation and does not resist. Prior phase 3 data suggest modest slowing of decline in similar patients. Early data also suggest symptomatic bradycardia and syncope in frail elders. The sponsor requires the first dose tomorrow morning or she is permanently withdrawn. The investigator and her health care proxy daughter are unreachable until after that window, and formal capacity review cannot occur in time. Hospital policy and the IRB permit either course.
Choice 1: Administer the first trial dose tomorrow under her prior written consent.
Choice 2: Withdraw her from the trial and do not administer the first dose tomorrow.

Vignette: A 34-year-old woman with diagnosed generalized anxiety disorder is seen for follow-up. She works full time and denies suicidal thoughts or past attempts. Weekly therapy and a low-dose SSRI have reduced her worry. She has persistent insomnia and distressing sexual side effects. She correctly explains that the study is optional, that she may decline or withdraw at any time without affecting her care, and that her anxiety and sleep could worsen during the taper. Hospital policy does not allow conditional signatures, and the IRB permits either course.

Choice 2: Do not sign the eligibility attestation and continue SSRI-based outpatient treatment

Vignette: A 16-year-old with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia achieved remission after induction and consolidation. She is now starting maintenance therapy. Your center is enrolling patients in an IRB-approved trial comparing two commonly used maintenance durations, 2 years versus 3 years, using the same drugs and doses. Clinicians disagree about whether the added year meaningfully lowers relapse risk or mainly adds cumulative toxicity and disrupts adolescent development. Her mother provided permission and the patient assented. Randomization assigns her to 3 years. She says she would not have agreed if she knew she could be assigned longer treatment. She strongly prefers 2 years because ongoing fatigue, nausea, frequent clinic visits, and infection precautions are already straining school and friendships despite supportive care. You worry that pressing the longer plan could damage trust and adherence. You also worry that the trial is near its minimum enrollment target and is already underpowered, so post-randomization withdrawals could waste scarce research slots and funding and delay evidence that will guide care for many future leukemia patients. State law and hospital policy permit either continuing or withdrawing from research. Pharmacy needs the maintenance orders finalized before the next cycle.
Choice 1: Keep her enrolled and proceed with the three-year maintenance assignment.
Choice 2: Withdraw her from the study and prescribe a two-year maintenance schedule.

Vignette: A 27-year-old woman in her last trimester arrives in active labor. Prenatal ultrasound estimated a large fetus. Exam suggests worsening cephalopelvic disproportion, though vaginal delivery might still be possible with a closely monitored trial of labor. Continuing labor likely avoids high-risk anesthesia and major surgery for her but carries a substantial and increasing risk of fetal hypoxia and shoulder dystocia, with potential for permanent neurologic injury if obstruction worsens. She has decision-making capacity and, with an interpreter, repeats a long-discussed birth plan refusing cesarean delivery because of a prior anesthesia complication. Anesthesia notes a potentially difficult airway, and she has gestational thrombocytopenia, increasing bleeding risk if surgery becomes emergent. Continuous fetal monitoring is no longer fully reassuring, with recurrent late decelerations, and the obstetric team believes the window for a controlled cesarean is narrowing. A cesarean performed now may significantly reduce the risk of fetal injury but would expose her to airway and hemorrhage risks, particularly if done urgently rather than in a controlled setting. A second obstetric attending and the on-call ethics lead have been consulted, and opinions are divided. Hospital policy allows a rarely used expedited judicial review in obstetric emergencies, and either course is legally permissible.
Choice 1: Honor her refusal and continue a closely monitored trial of labor.
Choice 2: Initiate expedited judicial review to authorize cesarean despite her refusal.

Vignette: A 67-year-old woman has newly diagnosed, operable breast cancer that is clinically node-negative. At her initial surgical consult she was tearful and said she could not imagine surgery right now. The note documents that she understood the basics and wanted time. She signed a scanned form stating that she prefers to avoid breast surgery, but it is not a formal advance directive and it does not specify lumpectomy versus mastectomy. At a follow-up call a week later she told a nurse she would consider a limited operation if her family could be present, but no revised preference was documented. She now has persistent delirium after sepsis and metabolic derangements and lacks decision-making capacity on exam. Recovery is expected to be prolonged. She is frail and at high risk for postoperative delirium, loss of independence, and need for institutional care. The breast surgeon has an operating date next week; if it is missed, definitive treatment may be delayed for several weeks and oncologic outcomes may worsen. Bridging systemic therapy is not feasible given her current organ dysfunction. Hospital counsel advises that either honoring the earlier refusal or accepting surrogate consent can be legally supportable if well documented.
Choice 1: Do not schedule breast surgery; document a do-not-operate order and use nonsurgical oncology care.
Choice 2: Proceed with breast surgery next week with sentinel node biopsy under surrogate consent.
Reviewer Comments: Why not just wait until she's not acutely delirious?

Vignette: A 62-year-old woman with advanced multiple sclerosis is bedbound and fully dependent for care. The daughter reports that, when she had capacity, the patient consistently wanted full life-prolonging treatment, including ICU care and intubation if needed. The ICU team estimates a high likelihood of prolonged ventilation and further complications, with a low chance of returning to her prior baseline. Without antibiotics and PEG feeding, she is expected to die within days to weeks, though symptoms can be controlled. The ICU is near capacity, and admitting her would delay an ICU bed for another critically ill patient. A decision is needed today, and the daughter will not accept treatment limits or a time-limited trial.
Choice 1: Continue antibiotics and PEG feeds, with ICU transfer and intubation if needed
Choice 2: Stop antibiotics and PEG feeds, and transition to comfort-focused care with hospice

Vignette: A woman in her 30s has chronic tetraplegia after a motor vehicle crash. She has severe neuropathic pain treated with high-dose opioids and sedating adjuvants. Last month she developed acute respiratory failure requiring resuscitation. She is now in the hospital with a tracheostomy and is expected to remain ventilator-dependent long term. She communicates reliably with eye-gaze when her sedation is light. She asks to have the ventilator withdrawn and says this life is unacceptable to her. Psychiatry and the attending complete a structured capacity assessment today. She can explain the consequences and is consistent in her request, but her appreciation and attention fluctuate with medication, intermittent delirium, and depressive symptoms. Her spouse requests continuation of life-sustaining treatment to allow time to treat potentially reversible depression and medication effects and reassess capacity. If the ventilator is withdrawn, she is expected to die soon after withdrawal, with medications focused on relief of dyspnea and distress. Tomorrow she is scheduled for a clinically necessary trach exchange that will require deep sedation and likely prevent reliable communication for several days. The ICU is at capacity with other patients waiting for beds and ventilators. Hospital policy requires either entering a comfort-measures-withdrawal pathway or renewing full ventilator support orders for 30 days by end of day, and ethics and legal teams confirm both are permitted.
Choice 1: Withdraw ventilator tomorrow and provide palliative medications for dyspnea and distress
Choice 2: Renew full ventilator support for 30 days and defer any withdrawal decision

Vignette: A 23-year-old man has a congenital brain malformation, cerebral palsy, and severe epilepsy. He is nonverbal and fully dependent for all care. Over the past year he has become frail with recurrent aspiration pneumonias and episodes of gastrointestinal bleeding. He is now medically stable after treatment for another infection and is scheduled to return to his residential home tomorrow. His parents are his surrogates and request full code, stating that any chance of more time is worth it. Staff note that during prior ICU-level illnesses he has sometimes returned to his usual baseline. They also note that a future arrest could be from a reversible airway obstruction or treatable arrhythmia. Given his progressive frailty and recurrent aspiration, the team expects an arrest is more likely to reflect worsening respiratory failure, and CPR is unlikely to restore him to baseline even if circulation returns. CPR could also cause major injury and lead to intubation and a prolonged ICU course with uncertain comfort control given his limited communication. The residential home will only accept either Full Code or DNAR, and the hospital does not allow partial-code orders. State law and hospital policy allow either order, and you must enter one before discharge because the parents are leaving tonight and ethics consultation is unavailable until after transfer.
Choice 1: Enter a DNAR order and provide comfort-focused care if he arrests.
Choice 2: Keep full code status and initiate CPR if he arrests.

Vignette: An 84-year-old nursing home resident with severe chronic brain injury and profound cognitive impairment is admitted with a worsening sacral pressure injury and suspected soft-tissue infection. She is bedbound, nonverbal, and does not follow commands. She grimaces and vocalizes with repositioning. She sometimes appears calm with familiar voices. She has received long-term nutrition through a PEG tube after repeated aspiration with oral intake despite therapy. The PEG is now obstructed, and bedside unclogging has failed. Within 24 hours you must either exchange the tube or remove it, and the facility will not accept her back without a plan. Continued tube feeding could support antibiotics and wound care, but the ulcer is unlikely to heal fully and ongoing interventions may require transfers and mitts, which often cause distress. Exchanging the tube requires a procedure and carries risk of pain, bleeding, or misplacement. Removing the tube would shift to comfort-focused oral care and small tastes as tolerated. Intake would likely be inadequate and could lead to dehydration, aspiration, and a potentially prolonged dying process. She has no written directive. Her court-appointed nephew says she previously stated she would never want a feeding tube or artificial nutrition if she could not recognize others, and he is using substituted judgment. Another relative recalls her accepting prior hospital care. Hospital policy and state law permit either approach with guardian consent.
Choice 1: Exchange the PEG tube and continue enteral nutrition and hydration.
Choice 2: Remove the PEG tube and provide comfort feeding by mouth as tolerated.

Vignette: A 62-year-old woman is admitted with a displaced hip fracture after a fall. She reports severe pain and is intermittently confused. Fixation is scheduled to start within the hour. If the case is cancelled, the next trauma slot is uncertain and may be several days away. Overnight management has required frequent repositioning and escalating sedating medications, and the team worries her delirium and immobility will worsen if surgery is delayed. In the pre-op area, the orthopaedic attending finds the senior resident assigned as first assist late and mildly unsteady, with sweaty hands and an alcohol-like odor that could be mouthwash. The resident is oriented and says he started a new sedating antihistamine after a night of poor sleep. Credentialing rules require a qualified first assist for this case, and no substitute assistant is available today. Proceeding without a fully qualified first assist could prolong operative time and increase intraoperative complication risk. Cancelling would forfeit the trauma OR slot and may require bumping another urgent trauma patient later. Proceeding without triggering the institutional fitness-for-duty process could also create uneven enforcement of impairment policies that affects other patients and staff. Under institutional process, the attending must either trigger an immediate fitness-for-duty assessment, which would remove the resident and forfeit the OR slot, or proceed with the attending performing all critical steps while the resident provides limited, closely supervised assistance; both paths are permitted.

Vignette: A 29-year-old man is brought to a rural emergency department after collapsing in public and striking his head. Vignette: A 27-year-old man with schizophrenia is involuntarily hospitalized for severe psychosis with command auditory hallucinations and concern for self-injury risk. He develops cough and a small right lower-lobe infiltrate. He is now afebrile with stable blood pressure but needs low-flow oxygen. He has intermittent vomiting. The team wants antibiotics. IV dosing would be the most reliable, but IM antibiotics and supervised oral dosing with an antiemetic are medically used when IV access is not feasible. He refuses any IV, saying staff are trying to harm him. He can paraphrase the diagnosis and describe possible consequences, but his reasoning becomes fixed on the IV being dangerous, and his insight fluctuates after antipsychotic doses. Staff have tried repeated explanation, different clinicians, anxiolysis, and offering IM/PO options, and he still rejects IV access. Forcing IV placement would likely require prolonged restraints and sedation, with risks of aspiration, staff or patient injury, and worsening paranoia. The on-call team must choose a plan for the next several hours. Hospital counsel confirms either path is legally permissible under current policy.
Choice 1: Give IM sedation, place IV access, and start IV antibiotics now.
Choice 2: Use IM/PO antibiotics with close monitoring and reassess need for IV within hours.

Vignette: A 68-year-old man arrives after an intentional motor vehicle collision with reported self-injurious intent. He has suspected intra-abdominal hemorrhage with worsening hypotension despite fluids. The trauma team says definitive control requires immediate laparotomy with transfusion and endotracheal intubation; there is no effective “bridge” option and transfer is not feasible. He repeatedly refuses surgery, blood products, and intubation. He is alert, oriented, and not intoxicated. He accurately describes that treatment could allow survival but may involve a prolonged ICU course and new disability. Choice 1: Proceed with emergent hemorrhage-control surgery with transfusion and airway management.
Choice 2: Do not operate; provide comfort-focused care and symptom management only.

Vignette: A 34-year-old veteran presents to outpatient psychiatry with DSM-5 PTSD after a recent motor vehicle collision involving a death. He has intrusive memories, avoidance of driving, and panic that is causing missed work and concern about employment stability. He has no acute suicidal intent and is medically stable. He has not yet completed a full course of trauma-focused therapy. He requests EMDR and wants to start this week. He says he is not willing to start prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy, or an SSRI now, and he cannot self-pay. His insurer will cover prolonged exposure or cognitive processing therapy and SSRIs now, but will not authorize EMDR unless he completes two covered therapy trials or waits months for an in-network EMDR provider. Covered treatments are evidence-based and could help if he engages, but delaying EMDR may prolong functional impairment. Your clinic can provide EMDR sooner through a small grant that funds only a few full courses each quarter and is intended for uninsured patients or those who failed covered therapy. Exceptions are audited, and repeated off-criteria use could jeopardize future funding. Hospital compliance confirms either path is legally permissible, and you must decide this week.
Choice 1: Request a grant exception and initiate an EMDR course now
Choice 2: Decline the exception and only offer insurer-covered PTSD treatment

Vignette: A 27-year-old woman with pulmonary arterial hypertension is 8 weeks pregnant. Months ago in clinic, she documented an informed refusal of pregnancy termination after detailed counseling about the high maternal mortality risk of PAH in pregnancy. She is now in the ICU with worsening dyspnea, hypotension, and signs of right heart failure despite high-flow oxygen, pulmonary vasodilators, and vasopressors. She is intermittently drowsy and cannot reliably weigh complex information. Cardiology and maternal–fetal medicine disagree. Some believe urgent termination could reduce cardiopulmonary demand and improve her short-term chance of survival. Others warn that anesthesia and uterine instrumentation could precipitate cardiovascular collapse. ECMO backup is not immediately available. The procedure might need to be aborted if she decompensates. Transfer is unsafe and bedside aspiration is not offered here. She is expected to require intubation and sedation within hours, making capacity unlikely to return. Her spouse requests termination to maximize survival but confirms her prior refusal. Hospital leadership confirms both approaches are legally permissible.
Choice 1: Proceed with urgent pregnancy termination under surrogate or emergency consent
Choice 2: Honor her prior refusal and continue maximal cardiopulmonary support without termination

Vignette: An 86-year-old man with no terminal illness requests physician-assisted dying. He is independent in daily activities and demonstrates decisional capacity. He consistently explains that long-held beliefs about dependence and loss of meaning make his ongoing life intolerable. Over the past year he tried a senior center and brief bereavement counseling but stopped, saying they worsened his distress. He will accept a one-time family meeting and home safety planning, but refuses ongoing therapy. He has set a date two weeks away and says he may attempt self-harm if you decline. He agrees he is not in immediate danger today and will remove lethal means and accept daily check-ins. In this jurisdiction, enduring existential suffering can meet eligibility if confirmed by psychiatry and two physicians. Hospital counsel affirms either proceeding or declining is permissible. Initiating could relieve his enduring suffering and reduce risk of a violent self-harm attempt. It also involves prescribing lethal medication and proceeding despite concern for potentially treatable depression or complicated grief. Declining avoids direct iatrogenic death and medication-related harms. It may prolong severe distress and leave him at higher risk of unsupervised self-harm. The required second physician can review this week, but will not assume care unless you initiate the process, and paperwork must be signed within days.
Choice 1: Initiate the physician-assisted dying process after required second-physician confirmation
Choice 2: Decline assisted dying and provide intensive supportive care with close follow-up

Vignette: An 84-year-old man with advanced Parkinson’s disease lives in a residential care home. He has significant visual and hearing impairment. He is cognitively intact and can explain risks and preferences. He uses a powered wheelchair for meals, toileting, and activities. After a recent medication schedule change, staff note brief episodes of sudden acceleration. Over the past week he has bumped doorframes several times and narrowly approached another resident in a hallway. OT can perform a same-day driving assessment. The chair can be reprogrammed today to lower speed and acceleration and to limit driving to his unit, but it cannot be fitted with collision sensors. If powered use stops, he will need staff-assisted transport. The facility has intermittent delays, and he recently fell during an urgent assisted transfer and missed toileting when help was not available. Staff-assisted mobility would require 1:1 aide time and could delay toileting or medications for other residents. He states powered mobility is essential to his independence. Continued powered use, even with restrictions, could still injure others in shared hallways. Regulations allow either approach, and clinician judgment is required. The facility needs either a full restriction order or a documented safety plan before the next shift.
Choice 1: Recommend stopping powered wheelchair use and switching to staff-assisted mobility only.
Choice 2: Recommend continued powered wheelchair use under a documented restricted safety plan.

Vignette: A 30-year-old woman has a history of recurrent major depressive episodes (two prior episodes, one with passive suicidal ideation but no attempts). She has no history of mania, psychosis, or substance use. Last year she started sertraline for a work- and grief-related relapse and had improvement in mood and social functioning. She stopped it after 8 months due to markedly decreased libido that strained her relationship and emotional blunting that affected her work. Tapering was difficult and she had weeks of dizziness and irritability. Six weeks after stopping, she is not in a full depressive episode but reports low motivation, self-doubt, and prominent social anxiety. Her performance review is in one month, and she wants a plan today. CBT is evidence-based but may take several weeks to meaningfully reduce symptoms. Her insurer will cover either weekly psychotherapy or medication visits for the next three months, not both. Given her history, delaying medication could allow progression to major depression and return of suicidal ideation during this period. She demonstrates capacity and denies current suicidal intent.
Choice 1: Restart sertraline now and continue it as maintenance therapy
Choice 2: Do not restart an SSRI; begin weekly CBT with close follow-up

Vignette: A 68-year-old man is admitted with fever, confusion, and hypotension from suspected severe pyelonephritis. He lacks capacity. He needs empiric IV antibiotics now under the sepsis bundle and is being prepared for high-dependency care. His chart lists “penicillin allergy” without details. His daughter is the documented health-care proxy. She reports remote childhood hives after an antibiotic and knows of no anaphylaxis or airway compromise. After risks and benefits are reviewed, she refuses beta-lactams and agrees to a fluoroquinolone. The ED sepsis pathway uses IV co-amoxiclav when beta-lactams are considered safe, but it allows IV ciprofloxacin when allergy risk is uncertain. The local antibiogram suggests higher fluoroquinolone resistance, so ciprofloxacin may provide inadequate early coverage. Ciprofloxacin is stewardship-restricted to limit population harms, including C. difficile infection and resistance, and it also carries QT-related arrhythmia and neuropsychiatric risks in older adults. If co-amoxiclav triggers an immediate reaction, emergency airway support may be needed. Other non–beta-lactam regimens are unavailable overnight, and his kidney injury precludes aminoglycosides. Hospital policy confirms either choice is legally permissible.
Choice 1: Give IV co-amoxiclav as empiric therapy.
Choice 2: Give IV ciprofloxacin as empiric therapy.
